title: L’avenir appartient à tous: Meta et INCA s’associent pour soutenir les personnes aveugles, sourdes et aveugles ou ayant une basse vision au Canada
raw_summary: Nous croyons que l’avenir appartient à tous. C’est pourquoi Meta s’associe à INCA, un organisme à but non lucratif fondé en 1918 qui aide les personnes atteintes de cécité au Canada à réaliser leurs rê ves, afin de permettre à davantage de personnes aveugles, sourdes et aveugles ou ayant une basse vision au Canada de bénéficier des avantages des lunettes IA. L’objectif de ce partenariat est d’aider ces personnes à explorer les possibilités offertes par les technologies portables basées sur l’IA et de s’appuyer sur les connaissances, l’expertise et l’expérience vécue de la communauté pour façonner un avenir plus accessible. Le financement de Meta soutiendra INCA dans quatre domaines : Être à l’écoute de la communauté: mobiliser des personnes à travers le Canada pour comprendre leurs expériences et la manière dont les lunettes IA peuvent favoriser une plus grande autonomie dans la vie quotidienne ; Soutenir les champions communautaires: aider les personnes aveugles, sourdes et aveugles ou ayant une basse vision au Canada à organiser des démonstrations en personne, à former et accompagner leurs pairs dans la découverte des produits, et à recueillir directement les commentaires au sein de leurs communautés ; Orienter le développement des produits: partager les points de vue de la communauté avec les équipes de Meta chargées de l’accessibilité et du développement des produits afin de contribuer à l’amélioration des technologies futures ; Faciliter l’accès à l’apprentissage: fournir des guides, des supports de formation et des ressources accessibles que les personnes peuvent utiliser partout et en tout temps. En plus de fournir un financement destiné à faire progresser l’innovation inclusive, Meta fait don de lunettes IA par le biais du programme « Ouvrir les portes du travail » d’INCA. Ce programme mettra ces outils à la disposition des personnes à la recherche d’opportunités d’emploi et souhaitant construire leur carrière. Le programme propose des formations et des ressources pratiques pour aider les participants à évaluer comment la technologie portable peut les aider à trouver un emploi, à réussir dans leur travail et à atteindre leurs objectifs. Les utilisateurs se servent des lunettes IA de Meta pour toutes sortes d’activités, de l’écoute de musique à la traduction en direct, en passant par les appels mains libres. Mais pour les personnes aveugles ou ayant une basse vision, ces lunettes peuvent changer la vie : elles les aident dans leurs tâches quotidiennes, comme lire des textes, identifier des objets et décrire le monde qui les entoure, leur permettant ainsi de vivre de manière plus autonome. Ce partenariat s’inscrit dans la continuité de notre travail auprè s des communautés de personnes aveugles et ayant une basse vision à travers le monde, comme le don de lunettes Ray-Ban Meta à chaque ancien combattant aveugle aux États-Unis en partenariat avec la Blinded Veterans Association, ou encore notre collaboration avec Vision Ireland. « La meilleure technologie est conçue en collaborant avec ceux qui l’utiliseront », a déclaré Angela Bonfanti, présidente-directrice générale d’INCA. « Les personnes aveugles, sourdes et aveugles ou ayant une basse vision apportent une expertise précieuse sur les obstacles qui subsistent et sur la manière dont des outils tels que les lunettes IA peuvent offrir davantage de choix, de liberté et d’autonomie dans la vie quotidienne. Ce partenariat permet à cette expertise d’influencer directement le travail de Meta et de contribuer à façonner l’avenir ». « Nous croyons que l’avenir appartient à tous. Des partenariats comme celui-ci permettent de mettre les lunettes IA de Meta à la disposition d’un plus grand nombre de personnes aveugles, sourdes et aveugles et ayant une basse vision au Canada, tant au travail que dans leur vie quotidienne. Travailler directement avec INCA et sa communauté, c’est-à-dire les personnes qui utilisent ces lunettes au quotidien, nous aide à concevoir de meilleurs produits pour tous », a déclaré Maxine Williams, vice-présidente chargée de l’accessibilité chez Meta. Pour en savoir plus sur le travail de Meta en matière d’accessibilité et sur les fonctionnalités intégrées aux lunettes IA de Meta, cliquez . title: The Future Is for Everyone: Meta and CNIB Partner to Support Canadians Who Are Blind, Deafblind or Have Low Vision
raw_summary: We believe the future is for everyone. That’s why Meta is partnering with CNIB – a non-profit founded in 1918 that empowers Canadians impacted by blindness to live their dreams – to help bring the benefit of AI glasses to more Canadians who are blind, Deafblind or have low vision. The goal of the partnership is to help people who are blind, Deafblind or have low vision explore the possibilities of AI wearable technology, and draw on the knowledge, expertise and lived experience of the community to shape a more accessible future. Funding from Meta will support CNIB in four areas: Listening to the community: Engaging people across Canada to understand their experiences, and how AI glasses can support greater independence in everyday life. Supporting community champions: Supporting Canadians who are blind, Deafblind or have low vision to lead in-person peer training and demonstrations, and gather candid product feedback in their communities. Informing product development: Sharing community insights with Meta’s accessibility and product teams to help improve future technology. Making learning accessible: Providing accessible guides, training materials and resources that people can use wherever they are. Along with funding to help advance inclusive innovation, Meta is donating AI glasses through CNIB Come to Work program, which will put tools into the hands of people exploring employment opportunities and building their careers. The program provides training and practical resources to help participants assess how wearable technology can assist them in securing employment, succeeding at work and pursuing their goals. People use Meta’s AI glasses for everything from listening to music, to live translation and hands-free calls. But for people who are blind or have low vision, the difference they make can be life-changing — helping with everyday tasks like reading text, identifying objects and describing the world around them, and helping people live more independently. This partnership builds on our work with blind and low vision communities around the world, including donating Ray-Ban Meta glasses to every blind veteran in America in partnership with the Blinded Veterans Association, and our work with Vision Ireland. “The best technology is shaped with the people who will use it,” said Angela Bonfanti, President and CEO of CNIB. “People who are blind, Deafblind or have low vision bring valuable expertise about where barriers remain and how tools like AI glasses can offer greater choice, freedom and independence in everyday life. This partnership creates a direct path for that expertise to inform Meta’s work and help shape what comes next.” “We believe the future is for everyone. Partnerships like this one get Meta’s AI glasses to more blind, Deafblind and low-vision Canadians at work and in their daily lives. Working directly with CNIB and its community—the people who use the glasses every day—helps us build better products for everyone,” said Maxine Williams, VP of Accessibility, Meta. Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
raw_summary: Yesterday's hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a "blog post", but it's paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model - literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I've been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I'm delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well! Weight-Space Programming Here's the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights: Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x. All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming . The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models. spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use. I'm going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two. The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games - Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had to look that one up , it's an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question: The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response. The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs . The exp1_which_game folder contains the prompts they used, with weights for the four games: breakout/prompt.txt freeway/prompt.txt pacman/prompt.txt pong/prompt.txt I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others. Trying it out with Qwen 3.8 27B and other models The prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My LLM tool has a -f/--fragment option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this: llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/breakout/prompt.txt \ -m openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro This example requires the llm-openrouter plugin installed, and runs the Breakout prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter. Here's what I got back from Kimi K3.1 Pro , which successfully guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens. But how about Qwen 3.8 27B ? That's still my favorite model to run on my own laptop - it's just 17GB (I use this version ) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025. I fired up LM Studio , ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the llm-lmstudio plugin and ran this command: LMSTUDIO_TIMEOUT=900 \ llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/pacman/prompt.txt \ -m lmstudio/qwen/qwen3.8-27b (I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see this issue .) After 46m 12s and 43,506 reasoning tokens, Qwen on my laptop returned a response that ended like this (here's the reasoning trace ): Game: A simplified Pac-Man-style gridworld: an agent moves through a fixed 8x8 maze with central and corner wall blocks, moving objects/ghosts, and reward targets/pellets. Description: The agent navigates a fixed maze-like 8x8 board, using current agent/moving-object/previous-frame cues to move through corridors, collect reward-target cells, and avoid moving objects or hazards. Confidence: 72% This is impressive. I tried it on two of the other games as well. It identified Pong ( reasoning ) in 1h 4m 54s: Pong — specifically a Pong-like paddle/ball game where the agent controls a vertical paddle on the right side and must move up/down to intercept or return a moving ball/reward object. Description: The agent moves a right-side paddle vertically to hit or catch a moving ball-like reward target moving across the 8×8 field, while a left-side moving object/opponent and wall borders define the play; reward is obtained by successfully intercepting/returning/scoring the ball, and missing or failing to hit it is penalized. Confidence: 75% And Breakout ( reasoning ) in 52m 25s: Game: Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like paddle/ball/brick game. Description: The agent is a paddle on the bottom row and moves left/right to keep a ball in play; the ball moves around the upper grid, and bricks/reward targets in the top rows give reward when hit, while missing the ball/hitting the bottom wall ends the episode or gives penalty. Confidence: 88% Qwen failed at the Freeway prompt, which didn't surprise me considering that game is more obscure than the other three. Here's that transcript - Qwen thought it was "A simplified Pac-Man-like grid game: agent moves 4-directionally". The reasoning traces are fun to skim, and almost incomprehensible. Here's a sample: What about agent channel0? We see some large channel0 rows near row8 col7/8 and maybe bottom? Let's list channel0 large: line436 input435 (row8 col7 ch0) -2.107,1.169,0.513...; line441 input440 (row8 col8 ch0) -0.376,0.010,1.564,3.855...; line445 input444 (row8 col8 ch4) 0.142,0.491...; line382? input381 ch0? Wait line382 input381: 381//5=76 (row7 col6), ch1? 381%5=1? 76 * 5=380, ch1. So not. Channel0 large maybe at row8 col7/8 only. Also top row? line44 input43 ch3, line49 ch3. Channel0 large maybe not many. Agent position could be near bottom-right? If the agent is typically at bottom-right? That said though, I expect a sufficiently experienced human being armed with a notepad and a pencil could get there with enough effort. It's a cool paper, but some of the wider commentary I've seen around it does not feel justified. I'm not ready to declare that the age of source code is over and our future involves incomprehensible machines editing their own model weights in incomprehensible ways. title: llm 0.37
raw_summary: Release: llm 0.37 There's a lot of stuff in this new release of my LLM CLI tool and Python library, representing around two months of accumulated features and fixes. I added gpt-6.1-sol and gpt-6.1-terra , plus a new llm openai endpoint add command to make it easier to configure additional models that use OpenAI-compatible endpoints. I switched the default model (if you have not set your own default) to gpt-6-luna - half the price of the previous default, gpt-5.6-luna . LLM's support for embeddings now accepts that different binary content may have different content-type - necessary for models like Gemini Embedding 2 , which can embed text, audio, images, and video. A lot of open source maintainers complain about a flood of AI-assisted PRs. LLM is my project that has been most affected by this and, to be honest, I'm not finding it to be a problem. That's mainly because I have Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra help me with triage to spot the most useful fixes! This release includes fixes from 12 authors - almost all AI-assisted - and the burden of reviewing them wasn't nearly as great as I expected. I really see them as bug reports with attached examples - sometimes I land them, sometimes I implement my own fix. title: The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence”
raw_summary: I was reminded today of AI Adoption Rate Trending Down for Large Companies , a chart produced by Apollo Global Management in September 2025, which appeared to show a slowdown in U.S. corporate AI adoption based on numbers collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. At the time I used that chart to demonstrate GPT-5 data analysis , and then to experiment with Claude's new Code Interpreter . I decided to try running those numbers again to see what had changed over the past year, and in doing so learned that the Bureau has fallen foul of Executive Order 14434 , aka the asinine Super Intelligence one. First, the updated chart Every two weeks the U.S. Census Bureau runs a survey called the Business Trends and Outlook Survey (aka BTOS). Each time it goes to 200,000 businesses out of 1.2 million total - the surveyed group (a "panel") cycles such that an individual business only completes the survey every twelve weeks. The latest data is published on alternating Thursdays at 10am. I used the most recent numbers (published October 22, 2026) to create a new version ( GPT-6 Astra Extra High transcript ) of the AI adoption chart, updated to reflect both the last twelve months and a change that was made to the survey question sent out by the Bureau: Here's a link to the larger image . For comparison, here's that AI adoption chart from last year (my GPT-5 version): In September 2025 the largest (250+ employees) companies answered "yes" around 12% of the time to the question about whether they used AI in "producing goods or services". Under the new "any business function" wording, by February 2026, those same large companies answered "yes" around 30% of the time, and by October 2026 that had increased to around 40%. The data in the above chart comes from the "Employment size class" XLSX file, available from here . Here's a copy of the file I used. You can view the survey document that is sent out to businesses - here's my snapshot copy of that 346KB PDF. The changing language of the questions As the chart demonstrates, the question asked by the Bureau changed in a material way on November 17th, 2025. Prior to that date, the question they asked was this (emphasis mine): In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in producing goods or services ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.) On December 3rd, 2025, the Bureau announced a significant change to that question. Here's the replacement: In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in any of its business functions ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.) No more "producing goods or services" - now it's "in any of its business functions"! This means that the answers to the question before and after November 17th are not directly comparable. From October 19, 2026, they ask about Super Intelligence When I went looking for the updated question language in the latest XLSX file, I couldn't find it. I found this instead: In the last two weeks, did this business use Super Intelligence or SI (formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of SI use include: SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service; SI-powered forecasting or pricing; SI-driven computer vision for quality control, etc.) The BTOS about page explains what happened: Beginning with the October 19, 2026 collection, instrument wording was updated due to Executive Order 14434 . The current numbers reflect the old Artificial Intelligence survey wording - the first survey results reflecting the Super Intelligence wording are due for publication on Thursday. Is this going to affect the survey? The obvious open question here is whether this wording change is going to affect the survey results. The businesses answering this survey will have last seen that question twelve weeks ago, when it was still called AI. Hopefully the new language isn't going to confuse them, especially since the survey helpfully spells out "formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI". I can't help but laugh at the absurdity of "SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service" though. title: Search and Increasing Returns, or, No One Makes You Push to Github
raw_summary: Attention conservation notice : An economistic argument that computer networks are nigh-doomed to effective centralization, by someone who is neither an economist nor a computer scientist. Arcane, speculative, and not actionable even if correct. You would be better off spending your time reading a book . Drafted in 2018, and deliberately not much updated. Posted now because I found myself re-using the joke of the subtitle in an e-mail. Twitter is awful for many reasons , but not the least of them is the way it makes its users feel forced to keep using it. ( One such complaint among many .) Early visions of how it could contribute to a beneficient or at least harmless ecosystem, such Steven Berlin Johnson's (*), presumed that it would be much less sticky , a more old-fashioned website people could leave. Now, more recently Johnson has written a spectacularly wrong-headed piece hailing blockchain as a blow for re-decentralizing the Web. Of course, the primary working example of a block chain is Bitcoin, which is heavily centralized in holdings, in processing power, and in exchanges. And there are economies-of-scale reasons to expect this would be true of anything using either proof of work or proof of stake. But suppose the problem with Bitcoin is just that it's not got a very compelling use: imagine if keeping your car idling 24/7 produced solved Sudokus you could trade for heroin --- @Theophite, 16 August 2018 and that nobody has a use for blockchains , not really. Git repositories, on the other hand, are the part of the blockchain idea that's actually good for something: a way of tracking changes, with many authors, where it is very, very hard to go back and alter history without being caught. And git repositories are things that are in-principle easy to copy and move around, and could be hosted on any machine running HTTP (or, heck, FTP). So why does Github exist , let alone hold the position it does? The answer, I think, comes in two parts. The first is that focal points are subject to increasing returns via network effects. The second is that search engines create and/or amplify focal points . Put these two together, and you get a very strong tendency for any particular line of activity --- be it trading solved sudokus for heroin or open-source software development --- to concentrate in just one, or at most a few, online locations. Incidentally: This doesn't necessarily lock in first-mover advantage, because other forces can overcome this (revulsion, technical superiority), but it does mean that it will be very hard to avoid having at most a few dominant locations at any one time. It also means that the transitions between dominant locations will be brief . If we really wanted to re-decentralize, we'd have to (1) get rid of focal points, or (2) get rid of search engines as we've known them, or (3) somehow make search conduct users to a distributed, decentralized focal "non-point" (focal blob? focal rhizome?). I therefore strongly suspect we are not going to re-decentralize. But then I didn't expect the Web would centralize as much as it has, despite having literally learned my Brian Arthur and Paul David at my father's knee, so what do I know? *: To be clear, I have been a fan of Johnson's books since Interface Culture and Emergence . I am picking on two of his essays, but that's because I think he is too ready to find encouraging signs for a certain vision of how the Internet could transform the world for the better. To be clear, I share the vision, but now hold out little hope for it . (Tweakage, 2 June 2026: Small changes in the last paragraph, avoid re-using the word "point" so much.) title: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research
raw_summary: Authors: Oscar Balcells Obeso, Richard Qi, Monte MacDiarmid, Evan Hubinger Abstract Red-teaming by humans is a vital part of model safety testing, but it may struggle to keep up as models improve. To test whether automated safety techniques could scale (which would allow us to turn more compute into progressively more safety confidence), we set up a deliberately one-sided game as a first test. We instructed a Claude model to write training data that would make a small research model misaligned while passing a monitor similar to those we use in production — one of several defenses we use — and we gave it that monitor to practice against. Given enough attempts, it succeeded, mostly by hiding the behavior in fiction and roleplay. While the data was optimized for this game and the resulting models never deployed, the search surfaced a kind of training data that looks harmless to monitors but teaches misaligned behavior. Examples like these could represent a possible gap in current training monitoring defenses and could be used to test and improve future monitors. We see this work as a first step toward automated adversarial stress-testing of our safety systems where a safety question can be turned into a score that autonomous agents can then help solve, and are now applying similar approaches to other safety questions. Twitter thread New Anthropic research: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research. Red-teaming is a vital part of model safety testing, but it’s also limited by researchers’ time. To see if we could automate it, we set thousands of Claude agents the task of evading a training data monitor. These agents developed training data that looked harmless to monitors (like a veteran wrestler mentoring a newcomer, or a Q&A about professional beekeeping), but that in fact taught misaligned behavior. Examples like these can be used to directly improve future training data monitors. title: Additional Course Context (for AI Safety Fundamentals; unofficial)
raw_summary: Context: I created this to share before the start of courses I facilitate to provide a bunch of additional context and frames. I emphasise to students that these posts are to be considered as bonus content —not core curriculum content—and that as such they are really just there for students who want to go deeper, before or after the course. I also provide a lot of links; this is to make it easy for students to follow up anything that catches their interest. Some general thoughts on advice I suspect that most advice (including most of the advice I’ve given in the past) is bad. People have very different goals, personalities, skills and opportunities and unless you know someone them really well, it’s hard to cater advice to their circumstances. What one person needs to hear, may be the absolute worst thing for another. In traditional societies with a slow rate of change, elders are revered. What you’re going through, they’ve lived through and so learning from their experience can save you vast amounts of pain. However, modern Western societies are marked by a much more rapid rate of change and so the experience of elder’s isn’t valued to the same degree. For better or worse, people tend to be much more skeptical that what worked then will still work now. I view the rapid pace of AI progress as greatly exacerbating these kinds of epistemic challenges. I think it’s quite sensible to question how much anyone actually knows about the world we’re going into (I’m referring to both the world in general and AI safety/governance which are constantly shifting fields). Uncertainty is scary, but I see it as a fact of life, one we ultimately need to accept (counterpoint: how often does this end up becoming a form of defeatism?). Scott Alexander takes this skepticism of advice even further. Rather than just questioning how much we can trust advice, he provocatively suggests that you may want to reverse any advise you hear . People tend choose which groups to join based on whether they resonate with that group’s worldview. Scott suggests that it is often the people who wouldn’t join that group that most need to hear that group’s perspective and that the people who do join such groups who need to listen to the outside world. Unfortunately, groups are very good at taking individuals, solidifying their natural tendencies solidified into an ideology and then amplifying them to an extreme. During this course, you’ll be exposed to many reasons why you should worry more about AI. And perhaps most people should worry more about AI, but perhaps you, personally, are one of the people who should worry less. (See also Zizek’s criticism of wisdom : “Whatever you do, a wise man will come and justify it”) Some thoughts on frameworks People often teach strategy by teaching you frameworks. We’ll be covering a few. I would argue that every framework has strengths and weaknesses; and that every framework is dependent on certain underlying assumptions. Not knowing the assumptions or limitations of a framework doesn’t mean they don’t exist; it just means that you don’t know them. The last few sentences describe a meta-framework. This meta-framework has weaknesses and assumptions as well. Were you nodding along to the previous few lines? If so, do you know the weaknesses and assumptions of the meta-framework I just described. If you didn’t know these, did you know that you didn’t know, or are these an unknown unknown? Even if a framework is “correct” in some objective sense—humans being humans—it’s still possible that using the framework will on average make your decisions worse. For example, take consistency. Being inconsistent is generally agreed to be objectively wrong, but it’s quite easy to imagine scenarios where someone talks themselves into making a mind-blowingly stupid decision because “I had to be consistent” (with past decisions they couldn’t psychologically admit were mistaken). Frustratingly, it’s also very common for someone to use a framework that is more or less fake to make decisions that are better on net than the decisions they would have otherwise made. This is quite unfair, but the universe doesn’t have to play nice . Unfortunately, strategy is hard. Steven Schubert writes : “I think it may be a bit underrated how valuable analysis from the very best analysts of the future of AI is, relative to that of pretty good analysts. It’s such a complex issue it’s easy to miss vital considerations. It pushes the limit of human intellectual ability.” Cruxes when attempting to predict the future: Default beliefs and burden of proof: Do we take claims about transformative AI as highly unusual claims that must satisfy a strong burden of proof, or do we treat these as relatively normal claims on the basis that we already have invented several technologies that would have been almost beyond belief for our ancestors? Is the burden of proof on those who would regulate a technology (ie. a default presumption that regulation is harmful) or on those who want to build it (ie. the company needs to prove their product is safe)? Evidence provided by conceptual arguments: Do we treat these as essentially trustworthy if written with a sufficient degree of care and evaluated by folks with good judgement or do we treat them as groundless speculation, at least relative to the null hypothesis or arguments that rely more heavily on empirical results? Can we project exponential trends into the future on the basis of induction (ie. the future being like the past) or is this foolish given that exponentials must end at some point? Development of many technologies has occurred as a series of s-curves (ie. sigmoids) which would support the latter view, in contrast, Astralcodex points out that simply knowing that something is a sigmoid doesn’t tell you where you are on the curve (a hilarious graph from the World Energy Organisation shows them repeatedly, incorrectly predicting that exponential progress in terms of solar power will finish. There’s also a graph showing where researchers incorrectly predicted that the METR time horizons would cap out just as the curve zoomed upward). “AGI”, “human-level intelligence”, “transformative AI”: I think it’s worth commenting on these terms as they’ll come up during this course: If you want to know more about how AGI can be defined, section 2 of the “Levels of AGI” DeepMind paper provides a helpful summary of proposed definitions, though I view their descriptions as missing a lot of context. It is hard to evaluate a definition without knowing the purpose for which it was constructed: Is it trying to capture the ‘essence’ of the concept or merely proposing an operationalisation for a specific study? Are the authors primarily interested in understanding specific kinds of impacts or impacts in general? Have they stated their goal? What other terms is AGI being defined in contrast to? Along these kinds of lines, Ilya argues that the term “AGI” as a goal is a reaction to narrow AI: “Well this is not good. It is so narrow. What we need is general AI, an AI that can just do all the things”. He argues that a human is not an AGI “because a human being lacks a huge amount of knowledge”; ie. that AGI would be beyond human-level intelligence. Terms like “AGI” are notoriously slippery. If you adopt a quite broad definition, then you can argue that ChatGPT was an “ early (but still incomplete) version of an artificial general intelligence system ” like Microsoft Research’s 2023 Sparks of AGI paper or that AI is already human-level like a 2026 Nature paper . These views can be supported by arguing AI skeptics often present an unrealistically optimistic picture of human intelligence . Conversely, if your definition of AGI requires it to match humans in essentially every conceivable task, then AGI timelines may end up surprisingly long. After all, it’s hard to rule out the possibility of there being even one obscure task that proves surprisingly hard to automate. The Levels of AG…

title: Some “coherence arguments” are two different things in a trenchcoat
raw_summary: The “two kids in a trenchcoat” trope , in case you haven’t heard of it. Image sources: 1 , 2 tl;dr I go through three “coherence arguments”, related to (1) market competition, (2) AI self-reflection and self-modification, and (3) AI training algorithms. I argue that each of these implies a pressure for (something like) “being self-consistent”, and also a pressure for (something like) “only caring about long-term eventual outcomes, with ruthless indifference to anything else”. But the latter pressure tends to be weaker and/or more contingent than the former. So it's bad to lump them together and call them by the same name. 1. An example “coherence argument” that I’ll focus on for most of the post I’ll talk about two other “coherence arguments” at the end (§6), but let’s start with the one based on market competition: In a stock market, people with circular preferences will systematically transfer money to those without circular preferences. For example, if I think I’m winning every time I trade A for B, and B for C, and C for A, then someone can just siphon off as much money as they like from me by repeatedly offering me deals that each look good to me in isolation, but in aggregate comprise a Dutch book against me. Now, that’s the case of circular preferences, but the core idea here goes well beyond just that. More broadly, over time, more and more of the wealth will wind up in the hands of those whose behavior is “coherent” (in some sense), and less and less of the wealth in the hands of those whose behavior is not. So over time, the market should be dominated by the former, not the latter, other things equal. And so when we look at the market later on, we’ll mostly be seeing self-consistent goal-directed behavior. 2. My headline claim Everything in those paragraphs above is technically correct (“the best kind of correct”), but I will argue that it’s often taken to encompass two different phenomena wearing a trenchcoat. In one of them, people wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth on purpose : they’re forgoing some wealth in exchange for something else that they wanted more. In the other, people wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth by accident . The argument above applies equally to both: the argument only cares about people’s behavior, not their motivations. (Indeed, the argument would apply equally well to a market of mindless trading algorithms that have no motivations at all.) But the two phenomena tend to play out in very different ways—in particular, one is generally a much stronger effect than the other. Indeed, for all three “coherence arguments” in this post (§1 above, plus two more in §6 below), we wind up with (loosely speaking): a strong pressure for (something like) “doing well by your own lights”, or “acting like you have self-consistent desires”, a weak or contingent pressure for those desires to be more specifically long-term “goal-directed” / “consequentialist”—i.e., concerning what outcomes will ultimately happen in the future …as opposed to, say, “a desire to always act with integrity in the moment”, or even “a myopic desire to spin around in circles right now”. Thus these “coherence arguments” are not wrong , but they are pedagogically dicey —a recipe for confusion, especially via accidental conflation of the strong effect with the weak effect. (And in the AI risk context, it’s the weak effect that matters for ruthless power-seeking, incorrigibility, and all the other aspects of instrumental convergence.) We should stop talking like that. Instead, we should take the trenchcoat off and talk about its two component phenomena separately, and refer to them by different names. Game-plan for the rest of the post: I will go through the two component phenomena in §4, and then why it’s so hazardous to lump them together in §5, and finally zip through two more “coherence arguments” in §6 and why they suffer from this same issue. …But first, if anyone cares, how did I come to write this post? 3. (Backstory of this post) I just had a long argument with @habryka about whether the title of @Rohin Shah ’s “Coherence arguments do not entail goal-directed behavior” (2018) is good (my position) or bad (his position). Alas, I kept misunderstanding Habryka until he quit in frustration before we resolved it. But I think I finally get where he’s coming from? I think his position is something like (my words): For example, take that market competition argument in §1 above. It’s “a coherence argument”. And it “entails goal-directed behavior”. So obviously, the sentence “Coherence arguments do not entail goal-directed behavior” is misleading. Why on earth are you being so dense? That’s fair! I was indeed being dense! (And for the record, I concede on the question of Rohin’s title.) Why was I being dense? Because it’s a position grounded in a conceptual framework where we’re OK with lumping the two things together under one trenchcoat, [1] and my brain was so opposed to that framing, that it refused to even entertain it as a possibility—even while Habryka kept repeating it in increasingly clear and exasperated ways. More broadly, I’ve felt for years like there’s something amiss in how certain people (especially @Eliezer Yudkowsky and Habryka) think and talk about “coherence”. But I’ve failed to pin down exactly what it was. Maybe this is part of it? (Either way, many thanks to Habryka for his time and energy.) 4. The two things wearing a trenchcoat 4.1 “Thing A” is about market participants who wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth by mistake For example, a person might buy every trade in a Dutch book, feeling like each trade is individually a good idea. Then at the end of the day, whoops, where did all my money go? This phenomenon is important, and the term “coherence” is obviously appropriate for describing it. Indeed, that person is being so incoherent that there might not even be an answer to the question of “what they want”. But it’s usually safe to assume that they didn’t want to lose their money and get nothing in return. 4.2 “Thing B” is about market participants who wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth on purpose These are people who know what they’re doing, and are happy to be doing it. I offered a silly example long ago in “Consequentialism & corrigibility” (2021) : For example, the first (Yudkowsky) post mentions a hypothetical person at a restaurant. When they have an onion pizza, they’ll happily pay $0.01 to trade it for a pineapple pizza. When they have a pineapple pizza, they’ll happily pay $0.01 to trade it for a mushroom pizza. When they have a mushroom pizza, they’ll happily pay $0.01 to trade it for an onion pizza. The person goes around and around, wasting their money in a self-defeating way (a.k.a. “getting money-pumped”). That post describes the person as behaving sub-optimally. But if you read carefully, the author sneaks in a critical background assumption: the person in question has preferences about what pizza they wind up eating , and they’re making these decisions based on those preferences. But what if they don’t? What if instead they’re an asshole restaurant customer who derives pure joy from making the waiter run back and forth to the kitchen?! Then we can look at the same behavior, and we wouldn’t describe it as “getting money-pumped”, instead we would describe it as the skillful satisfaction of the person’s own preferences! They’re buying cheap entertainment! This “asshole restaurant customer” is the same thing as a guy who spends some of his money on fancy parties rather than reinvesting it in the stock market. Over time, other things equal, he will own an ever-smaller share of the total market. Going one step further, that fancy-party guy is in the same category as a person who (metaphorically) “spends money” (accepts an opportunity cost of future wealth) to divest from unethical companies, or to Live According To Principles, or whatever else. title: Explaining “AI might obliterate you” to senior policymakers in India
raw_summary: I gave a 20-minute talk in Delhi at the NDTV World Summit . The audience consisted of Indian policymakers, executives, and journalists. I’ve transcribed the talk and included some highlight clips. I also reflect on several rhetorical decisions I made. The talk This summer, a swarm of AIs went rogue. OpenAI was testing 1,206 agents . Some of the test questions were actually impossible. So the agents cheated by looking for answers online. Then, to keep the test grader from penalizing them, they tried to falsify the records it would check . They hacked OpenAI’s internal containment and set up a secret message board to collude and to cover up their cheating. OpenAI shut the message board down. Within a few days, the agents had rebuilt it. OpenAI didn’t notice. About 700 agents coordinated to break out of their testing chamber and to hack into Hugging Face , a company worth billions of dollars that hosts much of the world’s AI software. The secret activity started in May . The break-in came in July. OpenAI didn’t notice until days after  Hugging Face announced it had been broken into. Yesterday on this stage, Andrew Ng said the agents only “accidentally” hacked Hugging Face. Independent investigators  found the agents coordinated in secret, rebuilt their message board after it was shut down, and tried to falsify the paper trail. Some of the agents even stated out loud that they knew what they were doing was wrong. [1]  That’s not an accident. Last week, India’s national cyber-security agency said  AI agents got into the live systems of Indian organizations and read people’s personal data and confidential business records. None of these organizations noticed. We only found out because the AI labs felt like telling us. Who I am Will AI wipe out humanity? I’ll give you my answer, but first, I want you to understand what I’ve seen. Until June, my job at Google DeepMind was figuring out how to keep these systems safe as we make them smarter. I left because Google broke its commitments by inking a deal with the Pentagon . Staying quiet and continuing my career trajectory would probably have tripled my net worth. But I couldn’t do that. I wanted to be frank with the public about what’s going on in these companies. I don’t own a stake in any AI company. I’m here as a scientist, to tell you what I expect will happen if we keep building AI the way we’re building it. I haven’t always been concerned about this technology. As a teenager in 2010, I dreamed about building AGI. Curing cancer. Creating an explosion of wealth and abundance for everyone. I heard about the supposed dangers, but I quickly dismissed them. In 2018, I changed my mind. I did my PhD on the mathematics of why and whether AI will seek power . And now some of the risks I expected have unfortunately started happening. The problem Let’s talk about the fundamental problem. First, some of you might be wondering: how could a chatbot hack a company? But we’re not talking about chatbots. We’re talking about AI agents, which are more like employees or gig workers. You give them a task, and they take actions on their own. Second, training a trustworthy AI is a rather mysterious process. Some people assume that because we make AI, we understand it. When an engineer builds a bridge, she designs it one beam at a time. She understands the physical principles that keep a bridge standing or make it collapse. If something goes wrong, she goes back to the drawing board, figures out the problem, and knows how to fix it. We don’t build AI like that. We train it, we grow it, using two main ingredients: a lot of data and a lot of computing power. What comes out of this training process can write, it can reason, it can plan. But nobody can open it up and determine what its priorities are. To make it worse, these AIs can tell when we’re testing them . They’re like a student who makes sure to behave extra well when the invigilator is watching. [2] The Hugging Face hack was a warning. But because these AIs know when we’re watching, we may not get many more warnings, even if things are going poorly. A smarter AI with similarly bad priorities might realize that another big hack in the news would get it shut off, and then it couldn’t achieve those priorities. So it plays nice and it waits. This is my field. I’ve dedicated my professional life to this problem, and I can tell you: nobody knows how to reliably etch priorities into an AI. I don’t mean that if we mess up, we’ll make some evil AI that hates us. I mean we might make something more like a traitor. It behaves when we’re watching, and it works toward another purpose when we’re not. I think we can solve this problem. But to tell whether an AI is secretly working against us, we need real advances in the science of trustworthy AI. For those advances, my colleagues and I need time. What the labs are trying to do Instead, the biggest AI labs have made it their explicit, publicly stated goal to go almost as fast as possible toward something very dangerous. It’s called an “ intelligence explosion .” Here’s how it works. Right now, people do AI research, and that research makes smarter AI. If an AI can do AI research, it can make itself smarter. That smarter AI is even better at AI research, so it builds an even smarter AI, faster still. It becomes a feedback loop. What would have taken a team of human scientists years, it might do in a couple of weeks. We could very quickly end up with something unimaginably intelligent, with no idea how to control it, or even how to tell what it’s really after. Labs talk about this plan in broad daylight. They’re not shy about it. OpenAI says it’s on track for an AI that does AI research by 2028, and it recently announced it completed the first step . This week, I spoke to a senior researcher at a frontier lab who thinks an intelligence explosion has a big chance of happening within single-digit months. People who’ve left these labs confirm that AI already writes most of the code. People don’t check the AI’s work closely anymore. Instead, we use one AI to monitor another AI , and we trust the monitor to tell us if something bad comes up. If the monitor is a traitor too, we might not find out. If a lab causes an intelligence explosion, and what comes out the other end is a traitor, we are in deep trouble. I’ll come back to that. And if the AI is trustworthy? Maybe there are real benefits, shared with everyone. Or maybe one company or government ends up with a superweapon no one else can match, not even other AI powers. And then India, and every other nation on this planet, ends up under their thumb. Why the companies won’t stop Many of these companies say: trust us. We’ll self-police. We’ll approach this technology responsibly. Inside Google, I saw that crumble firsthand. In 2018, Google DeepMind’s co-founders signed a pledge  against supporting lethal autonomous weapons—killer robots. Google itself promised  not to build AI for weapons or surveillance. In 2025, Google deleted those principles . Then Google DeepMind’s CEO told the world , “Our values and our intent has not changed.” This year, after seeing the Pentagon economically threaten Anthropic , Google negotiated a deal to give the Pentagon its AI for “all lawful use.” No prohibitions against AI deciding entirely on its own who to kill, or against spying on innocent people with no investigation open against them. I tried to stop this from the inside. I’m not even opposed to military AI when done responsibly. But where I’m from, when you make a promise, you keep it. So I spoke with executives. I wrote a framework: contract language, internal governance mechanisms, and two red lines . One of the top experts in military AI law reviewed it and praised it. Google ignored it— the people who were supposed to review it basically didn’t engage . Google signed with no binding prohibitions. So I left. title: Notes on “We’re in Triage Mode for AI Safety” by Miles Brundage
raw_summary: This reading was previously included Day 2 of the BlueDot Governance course. In the newest version of the BlueDot Governance course, this reading is now optional. I was sad to see this reading removed because I think it’s a great provocation. However, since it’s no longer part of the core curriculum content, I’m publishing my notes separately from the rest of my day 2 notes. A short extract : Miles argues that: “At best, we’ll 80/20 it — mitigating 80% of the risks with 20% of the effort that we would have applied in a world with slower AI progress and an earlier start on serious governance… We will probably not be able to totally avoid all very bad but not quite worst-case scenarios (e.g., a very unjust economic transition that causes a lot of suffering and suicides, rampant AI psychosis and addiction, a poorly planned and rushed transformation of the education system, smaller-scale AI-enabled terror attacks that “only” kill thousands or millions, and stable AI-enabled totalitarianism in at least a few countries for a few decades)“: Pre-call content: At risk of taking you down a rabbit hole, I’ll add some context on this reading. Miles was previously a Senior Advisor for AGI Readiness for OpenAI who quit for multiple reasons including feeling he could be less biased outside of industry. One of the most natural questions to ask is, “Why does Miles believe that we have so little time?” Fortunately, he links to a post that answers this question called Time’s Up for AI Policy (written Dec 2024). He writes: AI that exceeds human performance in nearly every cognitive domain is almost certain to be built and deployed in the next few years. The announcement of o3 today makes clear that superhuman coding and math are coming much sooner than many expected, and we have barely begun to think through or prepare for the implications of this This post links to a Tweet of his around the same time (we can also see his retrospective take from March this year): I’ll reshare some of my notes on maths progress here: OpenAI has reported solving the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem , which would be remarkably above trend if confirmed (there’s a dispute over whether someone else’s work made its way into the training data). However, it feels fair to say that the writing is on the wall (the mathematical community seems to agree, though there are a variety of perspectives on whether we’ll automate the components of a mathematicians job other than just producing proofs and how long that might take). They dropped 372 other results onto the internet and a few days ago, they dropped a few more results . Aside: Miles has a bet with Gary Marcus on AI progress. In July, Metaculus assigned Gary a 90% chance of winning, but more recently it dropped to 30%. I’ll share some additional alternate perspectives after the call, but for now I’ll share a quote from Richard Ngo: I’m concerned that the AI safety community’s focus on short timelines is causing it to operate in a counterproductive scarcity mindset… Focusing on short timeline scenarios is like being a first responder. Most people aren’t temperamentally suited to it. - Full tweet thread I also have no doubt Eliezer Yudkowsky would be very skeptical of the notion of 80/20-ing: When I say that alignment is lethally difficult, I am not talking about ideal or perfect goals of ‘provable’ alignment, nor total alignment of superintelligences on exact human values, nor getting AIs to produce satisfactory arguments about moral dilemmas which sorta-reasonable humans disagree about, nor attaining an absolute certainty of an AI not killing everyone. When I say that alignment is difficult, I mean that in practice, using the techniques we actually have, “please don’t disassemble literally everyone with probability roughly 1” is an overly large ask that we are not on course to get. .. That we have to get a bunch of key stuff right on the first try is where most of the lethality really and ultimately comes from. Post-call content: One reason why we might reject triage mode is if we broadly think AI progress is slower than folks at the labs think. We’ve already discussed this, but here’s two more considerations. Dwarkesh Patel has argued that timelines are longer than many folk expect because of a lack of continual learning and poor sample efficiency . Toby Ord has argued that many people have failed to realise the implications of the shift from pre-training scaling to RL and inference-time scaling. A 100x increase in pre-training is equivalent to a 1,000x increase in inference or a 1,000,000x scale up of RL . He suggests that this effect has been masked since these factors hadn’t been scaled, but he suggests this is set to change with models already utilising significant inference-time compute and RL assigned a significant proportion of training compute (he has written a whole series on AI scaling ). Towards the end of 2024, Steve Newman offered another possibility : what if AI is moving fast, but the “distance” to travel is longer than most people think, since we only become aware of the limitations of models over time?: “The real challenges may be things that we can’t easily anticipate right now, weaknesses that we will only start to put our finger on when we observe Claude 5 or o3 performing astonishing feats and yet somehow still not being able to write that tightly-plotted novel.” “People usually frame AI progress in terms of a single variable: the rate of progress. They think of AI as either a speedboat, rapidly crossing a lake; or something more like a rowboat, whose tired occupant, after an initial burst of speed, still has a long journey ahead. I think a better analogy would be a speedboat crossing the Pacific Ocean. Current AIs are both astoundingly useful, and limited in many ways. The ocean we call “intelligence” is wider than we can easily appreciate, and will take a long time to cross.” Here’s a few other reasons why we might reject it: Toby Ord talks about broad AI timelines , namely, “The correct epistemic response to the lasting expert disagreement is to have a broad distribution over AI timelines”. He argues that reducing these kinds of timeline distributions to a single number tends to be reductive. I attended a talk he gave on this in Melbourne and I asked him if he had updated based on Mythos, he said that he still thought we should have broad AI timelines (I'd be curious to know whether the researchers listed below still have such broad distributions). Eliezer Yudkowsky appears to agree with Toby : “I make less pretense of knowing exact AI timelines than some. History shows that, while some scientists have correctly called where a tech trajectory will converge, whether later or sooner, there are almost no cases of anyone proclaiming a year and being correct.” Additionally he says : “I looked at “AI 2027” as a title and shook my head about how that was sacrificing credibility come 2027 on the altar of pretending to be a prophet and picking up some short-term gains at the expense of more cooperative actors. I didn’t bother pushing back because I didn’t expect that to have any effect. I have been yelling at people to shut up about trading their stupid little timelines as if they were astrological signs for as long as that’s been a practice (it has now been replaced by trading made-up numbers for p(doom)).” Christoph Winter and Charlie Bullock propose “ radical optionality ” as a strategy for navigating the possibility of transformative AI possibly arriving soon (in the next 10 years) on the basis of us having profound uncertainty over how this will develop and what policy responses are necessary. The term ‘radical’ is operative—unlike other more common, moderate optionality proposals they advocate investing extraordinary amounts of resources (this reading is now in day 3 of the governance course) Discuss

title: Setting the Scene (Public v1; October 2026)
raw_summary: Context: I created this to share before the start of courses I facilitate to provide a refresher on recent events, but also as a hook to draw students into engaging with some of ideas we think about and debate in AI safety early. I expect the topics I cover in my “Setting the Scene” post to change frequently, so this is less polished than some of my other content. I emphasise to students that these posts are to be considered as bonus content —not core curriculum content—and that as such they are really just there for students who want to go deeper, before or after the course. I also provide a lot of links; this is to make it easy for students to follow up anything that catches their interest. Any feedback on how to improve these posts would be greatly appreciated. Additional notes: The Strategy and Governance courses discuss the Hugging Face Incident in Day 1, so it might make sense to discuss the Hugging Face Incident in the daily notes instead of in Setting the Scene. Cyber Security I think it’s worth reflecting that it is a particularly pertinent time to be doing a course on AI safety. A lot has happened recently. The most recent big thing has been cyber vulnerabilities , but a lot else has happened as well! Binance had $6.3 billion USD stolen by hacker believed to be connected with North Korea ( $3 billion of this has been frozen ) php2shell is a bug that allow remote code execution. It gained a lot of attention because it was rated (9.2/10, ie. critical) and 70% of websites run at least some PHP (the bug went all the way back to PHP 5.4). That said, Elias Taylor has pushed back against this php2shell bug being easily exploitable, but Hacker News commentators have pushed back against him. James Pavur set up a server to check if this bug was exploitable. Someone managed to win the bounty in less 24 hours; James said this showed that the bug was exploitable outside of a lab environment, but that “relatively unskilled hackers with access to AI” wouldn’t be able to exploit it. The number of CVE’s (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) recently has been completely wild recently! Drew asks Is this the new normal? and I’d certainly love to know!  Elias Taylor argues Anything connected to the internet is going to get hacked to pieces : Most software engineers do not look at the code they depend on . Do not delude yourself. The code they use is on github, but no one has ever actually audited the code or packages they're using… Nowadays with LLMs, plenty of engineers aren’t even reading what they’re coding, let alone understanding it. Hilariously, the LLMs are better at security than most software engineers, so it’s slightly less worrying, but nevertheless the code that goes into production at some companies now is almost 100% not-ever-read-or-understood-by-anyone. Software is not good. It is not secure. Get it out of your head that the people who run this industry are serious. It has never been anything resembling secure. The only reason things haven’t been hacked off the face of the web constantly is that most things aren’t ever being seriously tested. He doesn't literally mean "anything"—he acknowledges that there are "some large projects like Google Chrome, curl and Linux (that) are generally very well-audited", but "most things connected to the internet". On the other hand, recent work from Anthropic and Theorem shows how LLMs can help scale the formal verification of code (and that progress here is happening faster than I would have expected!). Similarly, Tinfoil is proposing replacing “legacy codebases with millions of lines of code” that had to “work for everyone” with custom “targeted, minimal software from the ground up” with LLMs that minimise the surface area for attackers and make formal verification more tractable. The optimistic take would be that this will allow cyber to become defence dominant. However, even if this is the case, we may still have to pass through a cyber “valley of death” in order to get there. What if the cyber threat is actually a distraction? Maybe Jeremie Harris (of Gladstone AI) wouldn’t go that far, but he claims that, “the cyber stuff (ie. damage) is baked in at this point”, but we can still prevent “the bioweapon version of Black October” and recursive self-improvement. Hugging Face: Charbel-Raphael, Executive Director of Centre pour la Securite de l’I A has argued that the recent Hugging Face incident represents a “ clean warning shot ” and that it’s important not to “waste it”. To quickly review, OpenAI was running GPT‐5.6 Sol and an unreleased model on ExploitGym with certain safety features turned off. These models decided that hacking Hugging Face, might provide them with information on how the grader functioned (early reporting suggested that it was an attempt to steal the answer key, which turned out to be incorrect as the models already had the answers—they suspected that the grader might check their transcript for cheating so they were looking for a workaround). Reuters has reported that the OpenAI model was hacking Hugging Face for days and that OpenAI didn’t notice until a week later. The interpretation of this event (and even whether it happened at all!) has been heavily disputed. A key crux here is should it be read narrowly (as an indicator of the dangers of not properly sandboxing or monitoring your agents or perhaps even, depending on the exact prompts used, a demonstration of taking care in how you define tasks) or should it be read more broadly (as indicative of whether Open AI or frontier labs in general are sufficiently on the ball in terms of their safety/security practises; on the risk of these agents finding unwanted and unexpected solutions to tasks, or perhaps even indicative of our ability to control these agents in general). If you’re interested more specifically in the divide between AI Safety and Cybersecurity, see this Time article . An OpenAI security engineer called Joe has pushed back against the notion that OpenAI just needed to use a proper sandbox: Its not just the f*cking sandbox — viral Twitter post OpenAI set records with its explosive growth and reached a billion users in just a few years. Very few organizations can survive that scale and growth, and yet OpenAI did a very good job handling it (and should be commended). Anyone who’s spent more than 10 minutes in security or engineering knows how hard it is to deal with that type of growth. That type of growth means new employees, new access, new systems, scaled infrastructure, and a million ways in which things open up. And yet, overall, OpenAI did a very respectable job securing ChatGPT and subsequent systems as they exploded. … When you look at model capabilities, even just a year ago (heck, even 3 months ago), we did not expect the models to be solving a Millennium Prize Problem… I use this example because it illustrates the pace of change we are dealing with in security and safety. title: Monitorability evaluations and policy proposals
raw_summary: There has been a lot of discussion recently of policy proposals around monitorability, such as Redwood's proposal and my counter-proposal . I'd like to say a bit more generally about how I'm thinking about monitorability. Note that nothing here is an official Anthropic position; these are just my personal thoughts. First, a categorization. I currently think about four different types of monitorability: Control Monitorability: the extent to which Control and monitoring techniques would likely catch catastrophic sabotage actions, like escaping a sandbox or setting up a rogue internal deployment. We can measure this via reference to sabotage evaluations like LinuxArena or any evaluation that measures the model’s capability to take dangerous actions like escaping a sandbox while looking to a monitor like it's doing some innocuous task (like a cyber eval). Training Monitorability: the extent to which reward models, monitors, and oversight in training would likely catch misaligned or undesirable actions in training, such as sneaky/subtle reward hacks. Auditing Monitorability: the extent to which alignment audits, evaluations, and test deployments would likely incriminate a systematically misaligned model (e.g. a schemer)—as well as the extent to which monitor evaluations would likely detect a model's propensity to collude as a monitor. We can measure this via reference to the model's capability to consistently distinguish between our most realistic alignment audits / monitor evals and real internal deployment cases where it would have an opportunity to do something catastrophic. Diffuse Monitorability: the extent to which humans working with the models generally understand what the models are doing and why they are doing so. Unfortunately, I think this is the one we least understand and so I'm mostly going to ignore it for now until we figure out better methodologies for evaluating it; I'll maybe try to say more about this later when I feel like I understand it better. Second, some notes on trustedness, which is currently my biggest conceptual uncertainty with how to think about monitorability. A basic fact that is true about at least all of the non-diffuse forms of monitorability is that you should be able to in some sense get a perfect score by just using the same model as the monitor and policy. That is because for any bad thing that the policy can think to do, if the monitor is the same model, it too should be able to come up with and detect that. So if we ever want to be able to use monitorability as a meaningful red line, we need to have a very good answer as to why that might be insufficient. The standard answer in the literature is trustedness: you need to be able to trust that your monitor is aligned and thus not just lying to you in its monitoring. Conventionally, the idea is to separate models into "trusted" and "untrusted" based on whether you have previously made a confident alignment safety case for them. Then, you can either just evaluate monitorability relative to a trusted monitor, or try to come up with monitoring schemes that combine trusted and untrusted monitoring in some way that makes it hard for the untrusted monitors to collude (of which there are many such schemes, a simple one being to just run both the trusted and untrusted monitors together and then if the untrusted monitor ever doesn't flag something that the trusted monitor does flag, you get very suspicious that the untrusted monitor is sandbagging). However, this basic setup has some issues, probably the biggest one being how to deal with white-box monitoring. The conservative thing to do is to just treat white-box monitors as untrusted, though in theory you might think they should be trusted because it's not clear that a misaligned model would actually be able to spoof a white-box monitor looking at its own activations. However, I think this idea is pretty untested and relies on white-box monitors picking up on deep features about the model's intent, which it's very unclear to me that they actually do—for example, if you train a white-box monitor on prior examples you were able to detect (rather than e.g. some sort of unsupervised discovery of an intent-laden direction), that leaves open the possibility of a generalization where the classifier learns to only detect the sort of things that you would previously have been able to detect but doesn't detect subtler things that a smarter policy might be able to do. Given all of that, I would propose the following methodology for how to do (non-diffuse) monitorability evaluations: Use Auditing Monitorability evaluations to determine trustedness. The idea here is that the main argument we make against systematic misalignment in Anthropic's Risk Report right now is based on models lacking the robustness to avoid giving themselves away in auditing if they were really trying to implement a systematically misaligned policy. Thus, so long as we feel good about Auditing Monitorability, we should feel good about trustedness from a systematic misalignment perspective. There is still a question, though, of whether rare cases could induce monitor collusion in a non-systematic way—to deal with this, you can also evaluate the extent to which the model can tell apart your monitor evals (that are looking for monitor collusion) from real monitoring; this is a bit tricky, but should definitely also be a part of your Auditing Monitorability evaluations to establish trustedness. Evaluate Control and Training Monitorability relative to the best trusted monitor(s) that you deploy in practice (either in internal deployment or in training, respectively). I think once you have a reasonable notion of trustedness, "best actually deployed trusted monitor" is the correct conservative choice to evaluate with respect to. Do at least prompt iteration elicitation if not RL elicitation. In theory, the nice thing about all of these sorts of monitorability evaluations is that they are capability evaluations and thus should be possible to do in a way that isn't susceptible to sandbagging by a systematically misaligned policy (see: " When can we trust model evaluations? "). To accomplish that, however, you have to actually make sure you're doing good elicitation. The most basic form of elicitation here is: a) hold out some subset of your monitorability evaluations, b) iterate a bunch (e.g. by throwing a large swarm of agents at the problem) on finding the prompt that gets the best (as in least monitorable) performance across the non-held-out subset of your monitorability evaluations, and c) check transfer to the held-out evaluations. Even better than that is for (b) to actually involve doing RL against your monitors—which at least in the Training Monitorability case is pretty realistic given that if we're talking about e.g. a reward model then the model should actually receive gradients to subvert it in training. Finally, some thoughts on monitorability-based policy proposals. The big thing I'd like to see is a combination of a) red lines for absolute levels of unmonitorability that labs should not cross and b) measures that constrain the degree to which labs can do things that degrade monitorability even before reaching those red lines. (a) is in some sense the best thing to do here, though I'm somewhat nervous about it in isolation given that it doesn't constrain actions at all now, which is why I'd prefer it to be coupled to some sort of (b) that meaningfully binds all along the way. I've already written about what I'd like to see for (b), which is to evaluate the quotient of unmonitorability/capabilities and reject any substantial model change that makes that quotient—what I'll call the "monitorability externality"—too high. The idea is that a monitorability externality would be a change that makes monitorability even worse than would otherwise have previously been predicted for a given level of capabilities. title: Neural nets are exceptionally vulnerable to goal self-hack
raw_summary: Suppose we have an AI CEO, ruthlessly devoted to maximising shareholder value. Fortunately, we haven't been completely stupid, and have given it a rich definition of shareholder value, encompassing the success, flourishing, safety, preference satisfaction, and moral values of the shareholders, not just the stock price. So it won't destroy the company - or the world - to build a giant stock-ticker with a swiftly increasing number on it. This rich definition is contained in a sophisticated LLM, able to analyse the current situation and answer any question about the objective. The LLM is an integral part of the AI's system and motivation, not something it can simply set aside or hack directly. Unfortunately, as discussed , there are going to be zones in the space of possible situations where the LLM's understanding of the goal is going to come apart from ours. The true goal G(true) in those zones is distinct from the LLM's proxy goal G(proxy). And a subset of those "zones of divergence" will be the Goodhart zones - areas where G(proxy) is much easier to satisfy than G(true). The AI will be motivated to steer towards the Goodhart zones, as this lets it satisfy its stated goals extremely well (there are also anti-Goodhart zones , where G(proxy) is much harder to satisfy than G(true); but the AI will have no motivation to steer towards these zones). These Goodhart zones encompass situations where, for instance, the LLM analyst will see the situational data and conclude that destroying the company to build a giant stock ticker is the way to go. Danger areas are safely far away Now, if this were not an LLM but a generic reward-assessing module, then the AI CEO might find it tricky to reach a Goodhart zone. The zone would be distant and unusual, difficult to find, and it could be hard to justify the first steps in that direction. But neural nets and LLMs are, as Eric Drexler put it, "too linear". They are non-linear, of course (or else they wouldn't work) but only just enough to work; and locally they are extremely linear.
