title: How a Kenyan Startup Is Rethinking AI for Small Businesses
raw_summary: The first time Mutembei Kariuki thought about how AI models could work in Kenya, his home country, was in 2019. He was attending a conference at the University of Tokyo on the future of AI, and kept hearing about how this technology was going to transform the world. “But nobody mentioned Africa at all,” he says. Even then—before AI giants like OpenAI and Anthropic had launched their chatbots to the public—Kariuki could see significant obstacles to AI adoption in Africa. Internet access was slow and unequal, computing resources for training models were scarce, and there was little high-quality, structured training data. Most people, meanwhile, reached the internet through outdated, low-memory cellphones rather than computers or high-end phones. Together with co-founders Jude Mwenda and Stephanie Njerenga , Kariuki created Fastagger , a start-up that builds AI models that can run offline and on low-power cellphones. Its first big product, Auni, is a business intelligence assistant that launched in 2024; it got a big push when it was integrated into the business app of M-Pesa , Kenya’s largest mobile money service. Since then, about 6,000 businesses have signed up. Auni helps small and medium businesses like barbershops, restaurants, and small manufacturers analyze their transaction data and gives them marketing recommendations. Peter Chege, owner of a salon and barbershop in Nairobi, started using Auni last year. Before that, he recorded all his sales on paper. “We were not able to translate that information into a graph,” he says. Now, the app helps him identify his busiest days and hours, as well as his loyal customers. If a regular customer stops coming, for example, he can send a personalized message encouraging them to return. Fastagger is part of an emerging effort to build AI around the technological realities of users in developing economies, rather than adapting products designed for wealthier markets. In Fastagger’s case, that meant finding a way to make their models work despite inexpensive phones, unreliable internet connections, and business records that may consist of little more than mobile-money transactions. Designing AI for Kenya’s Small Businesses Before developing Auni, Kariuki and his co-founders started by tackling the problem of data availability for AI training. They asked themselves: “How do we get Africa to catch up fast? How do we create training data fast enough, and then how do we actually get it into people’s hands fast enough?” Mutembei Kariuki cofounded Fastagger to develop AI systems that can run offline and on basic phones. Afrikanna Production/Microsoft They decided to focus on mobile phones, and specifically on mobile money apps. With more than 80 percent of Kenya’s adults using them, they offer a rich source of data. One of Fastagger’s first steps was to adapt an open-source optical character recognition (OCR) model to read financial statements produced by mobile money apps. Existing models struggled with the low quality of the PDFs, which had unfamiliar formatting and sometimes contained stamps and errors. And because Fastagger’s prospective users often had unreliable internet connections, they made sure key steps, like organizing the extracted data into tables, could run on-device. Once they had a model that could process these documents, they began exploring how that structured financial data could help businesses. They spent entire days watching small-business owners work and interact with their customers. One challenge quickly became clear: Owners had little time or resources to think beyond day-to-day operations. “They are standing up the whole day cutting hair,” Kariuki says of salon owners, who are now among Auni’s main users. “You have to think about that dynamic of the user journey, and how they live, and what will be going on in the background.” The Fastagger app helps salon owner Peter Chege better manage his time and keep track of loyal customers. Afrikanna Production/Microsoft For Chege, one of Auni’s biggest benefits was helping him manage his time. A simple chart showed him that mornings were his slowest hours, so he realized that he could run errands then or keep fewer barbers in the shop until around 1 p.m., when business picked up. The founders also saw how much time businesses spent on manual processes and how automation could simplify those tasks. At a fish restaurant in Nairobi, for example, identifying loyal customers to offer them discounts required going through SMS sales receipts one by one, a tedious task that rendered client-retention marketing impractical. Now, with the help of Auni, the restaurant identifies its top customers automatically and offers them discounts. Some of Auni’s functions—such as reading sales statements, analyzing data, and visualizing results—can happen offline on low-cost phones, without making cloud queries. These functions involve both AI tools and conventional software; for example, standard OCR software extracts the text and a small neural network identifies how each document is structured. More detailed analyses and answering questions about the data, however, require an internet connection. Daniel Björkegren , an economist at Columbia University who studies AI’s implications for developing economies, says sub-Saharan Africa’s prevalence of basic phones rather than smartphones and computers could open the door to different kinds of AI use. “The history of technology should suggest that this is not going to be people running Claude Code or Codex on their laptop,” he says. “You will have people like that, but for much of the population, we’re going to have to figure out different usage modalities.” How Local Needs Are Shaping AI Despite Auni’s integration into M-Pesa, Fastagger remains a small startup. It has received support from Google, Microsoft, and NVIDIA accelerator programs, but still has just three employees: Kariuki, Mwenda and Njerenga, the original founders. Currently, they’re working on adding agents to Auni that could automatically implement marketing actions for business owners. Fastagger has also developed a workforce management tool for Kenya’s security companies, which employ hundreds of thousands of people. Security guards often work in remote locations without reliable internet and use low-end phones. Fastagger’s AI agent communicates with them via SMS to track their routes, detects anomalies, and generates actionable alerts for operations teams. Fastagger isn’t alone in tailoring AI models for the usage conditions in emerging economies. Other examples include an app for rural schools without internet in Chile ; a medical triage chatbot for rural patients in India , and translation models for African languages that run on basic phones . Such innovations, which emerge from constraints, could help democratize access to AI. But that doesn’t mean the constraints themselves disappear or stop limiting development. While Björkegren sees great potential in systems built for populations that have been poorly served by Silicon Valley, he believes there’s a risk in establishing too clear a division between small models designed for emerging economies and increasingly large, powerful models for wealthier regions. “I am worried that that could lead to a bifurcation,” he says. “We need to enable a large menu of different options and really make sure that we have access and then see what works.”

title: Guarding the Gates of Knowledge
raw_summary: A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion. Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must. Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “ I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper ,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses. “He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.” Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it. Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions , Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup , a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools. “Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.” If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty . Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity. Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

title: Consumer Appetite for Personal AI Goes Mainstream
raw_summary: This article is brought to you by Qualcomm Technologies . For many consumers, much of the promise and appeal of AI is personal. Consumers are looking past generic tools and want to know how these technologies will help them in their daily lives. These trends coincide with the advent of new classes of wearable devices that, in addition to being able to leverage powerful frontier models, feature built-in intelligence that understand the context of a user. Where are they? What are they seeing and hearing? What are their habits, their preferences, their schedules? It’s an astonishing pivot, from passive accessories that served mostly to send users smartphone notifications to proactive, intelligent companions. The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI. And it shifts the focus toward you, the user. These new technologies are exciting. But what do consumers really want? A Personal AI report , commissioned by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide (the U.S., U.K., Germany, India, Brazil, and China) focused on the rise of personal AI in intelligent wearables looks deeply at these developments. The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI. Survey respondents are less interested in single devices and are responding more to the idea of connected ecosystems. As people expand their roster of devices, it only makes sense. Instead of relying entirely on a smartphone and a laptop, respondents also have connected technology in their cars, as well as intelligent wearables like smartwatches, smart glasses, hearables, and other wearables like rings, pins, and pendants. They want those devices to work in concert, and the way to do that is to decentralize any single one of them. Instead, the AI agent that knows the user and works across all of those devices becomes the unifying factor. Consider a typical workday: A user’s watch detects it is time to leave for a meeting and, with permission, their AI agent factors in calendar details, real-time traffic and battery status across their devices. In the car, it suggests the best route and briefs them on their meeting agenda. As they arrive, smart glasses surface a discreet reminder, such as the meeting location or the name of a new contact, while the phone stays in their pocket. No one device has to do everything; each plays the role it is best suited for, coordinated by a personal AI agent that understands the user’s context and acts only at the user’s direction. With this in mind, simply adding more hardware to the mix isn’t sufficient. Even though respondents will be open to new form factors, they’ll demand more from their ecosystem of devices. They’ll be sensitive to points of friction and needless complexity, and they’ll require each new device to bring something new to the table — “incremental intelligence, convenience, or contextual awareness that their existing devices cannot deliver on their own what the report,” reads the report. The usage trends are up. The report found that those who own wearables are already using AI frequently (60 percent use it at least weekly), which indicates that it’s becoming less of a fun experiment for early adopters and more of a critical mass habit. The “always-on” nature of intelligent wearables appears to be winning respondents, too. The report found the following statistics on average continuous wear among users: True wireless earbuds – 3 hours Wireless headphones – 3 hours Smart glasses – 5 hours Audio glasses – 6 hours Smartwatches – 9 hours Smart rings, necklaces and pendants – 8 hours Consumers want AI that is personal and understands their context — they’re looking for smooth, intuitive experiences that are marked by privacy, security, and user control. Consumer Trust Is Hard-Won But for all the excitement and engagement around intelligent wearables, there’s a gating factor: trust. As use cases for intelligent wearables expands to more personal and persistent experiences, trust is a necessity for Personal AI. The top reported issues around adoption are privacy, security, and user control. The data points to a certain amount of caution around deeply personal use cases, like voice, health, and location, as almost 60 percent of respondents want to keep data from their wearables private, or at least insist on gaining approval before it gets shared. In other words, even though premium features like high-quality audio, perception sensing, battery life, and comfort whet consumer appetites (and agentic AI capabilities drive upgrade intent), true adoption will come only with consumer trust. They want security, privacy, transparency and control. Notably, the report found that respondents expressed more interest in adopting intelligent wearables when Snapdragon was introduced as the enabling platform. This reinforces the value of having an established, trusted technology foundation in the mix. The Industry Remains Fluid The report shows that consumer appetite for AI is high, with 60-70 percent of those surveyed expressing interest in advanced AI as they consider a new device. That’s a constant. But remaining purchase drivers differed between device categories. Audio playback quality is the most influential purchase driver for true wireless earbuds and headphones. For smartwatches, it’s display quality and responsiveness. Respondents are less concerned about technical specifications than aesthetics like materials and finish when it comes to devices like smart rings and pendants. And for smart glasses, it’s all about the type of control, whether it’s voice, gesture, or touch. aspect_ratio The Rise of Personal AI in Intelligent Wearables Artificial intelligence is entering a new phase, one that is deeply personal, continuously present, and seamlessly embedded into the devices we wear every day. This evolution, which we define as “Personal AI”, represents a shift away from generic, cloud-only intelligence toward AI that understands individuals in context: their habits, preferences, environments, and intent, in real time. Get the full report → Alongside these purchase drivers is another key finding: Consumer appetite for Personal AI agents has gone mainstream. The report says that 70 percent of respondents “express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.” With each individual as the center of their own ecosystem, voice becomes the most critical, natural method for interacting with agents. The Opportunity The industry for intelligent wearables is exciting. It’s clear that consumer demand for Personal AI is high, and this report dives deeply into the specifics of what respondents want out of it. They want AI that is personal and understands their context, and they want it to be proactive and helpful instead of merely reactive. They’re looking for smooth, intuitive experiences that are marked by privacy, security, and user control. Intelligent wearables comprise much of the hardware of this “ecosystem of you.” Consumers are interested in ecosystems instead of single devices, and they’re looking for agentic AI capabilities that understand and act on their behalf. Yet so much of the industry remains undefined. OEMs and technology makers have an enormous opportunity right now to innovate and iterate on the strong technological foundations that platform makers are building. And the roadmap for what consumers want is clear. title: Systems Thinking Is Vital in the Age of AI
raw_summary: Modern engineering projects increasingly combine human judgment with machine capability. An engineer can define a problem, then ask an artificial intelligence tool to search relevant research and technical standards, generate design options, test them in simulation, and compare the results. The engineer can then bring the results to specialists who understand the parts AI cannot judge on its own, such as whether a design can be built safely, whether it makes sense in a particular setting, or how it might affect its users. The final decision about whether and how to move forward remains a human responsibility. AI can help engineers do early project steps that once required several people with different technical skills. The engineer’s role is therefore expanding from performing each technical step to deciding how people, machines, and specialists’ knowledge should work together on the project. The problem, not the title Engineering has always been divided into disciplines, and for good reasons. Electrical, mechanical, civil, software, and other engineering fields require deep knowledge that takes years to develop. AI does not replace that need. It simply changes how easily engineers can explore the parts of a problem that sit outside their own specialty. Consider a software engineer working on a medical device . AI can help the engineer review relevant biomedical research, understand unfamiliar terms, analyze data, and build an early model. That does not make the engineer a physician or biomedical expert. It allows the engineer to ask better questions before working with the experts. The same is true in energy , transportation, manufacturing, and many other fields. A problem might begin as a software issue and then quickly involve hardware, safety measures, economics, human behavior, and regulations. Engineers do not need to master every field; they need to recognize which expertise the problem requires and bring the right people and tools together. The importance of systems thinking Systems thinking thus becomes especially important. It requires looking at the whole problem: understanding how its parts affect one another, identifying constraints and failure points, and making trade-offs. AI adds a new element to the process. Engineers must decide not only how the technical parts fit together but also what work to give to AI, what a person must check, when a specialist should make a decision, and when the problem needs to be redefined. An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project. This aspect is crucial because technical challenges in engineering are seldom static. As new insights emerge, objectives might shift, unseen limitations can surface, and the initial premise might prove flawed. Rather than rigidly following the starting specifications, an effective engineer adapts and refines the scope as a deeper understanding of the system develops. Thus, engineering extends beyond mastering technical concepts; it is an adaptable, structured approach to navigating evolving challenges. New evidence can change the goal, reveal a hidden constraint, or show that the original hypothesis was wrong. Effective engineers go beyond merely acting on the initial problem statement. They update it as the system becomes better understood. In that sense, engineering is not only a body of technical knowledge, it is also a disciplined way of thinking about a project. Human judgment is important AI can produce convincing answers even when its assumptions are weak. It can generate code that works in one test but fails in another. It can summarize research without understanding which evidence is strongest, or optimize a design for the wrong goal. Such limits make human expertise more important, not less. Machines are useful where speed, scale, search, pattern recognition, and data generation matter. People are essential where context, values, responsibility, and judgment matter. The challenge is to decide where each belongs. An AI system might generate several designs for a medical sensor, for example, and predict how each will perform. An engineer can test the predictions and reject designs that violate technical requirements. A clinician can determine whether the sensor can be realistically used. Patients and practitioners might reveal problems that neither the engineer nor the developer considered. The final solution emerges from combining the perspectives. The engineer is still a builder and specialist but increasingly also a coordinator of knowledge. An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project. IEEE’s vital role The broader form of engineering creates an important role for IEEE. Its societies already bring together expertise in various technologies, engineering education , technical standards , and other fields. That makes IEEE well placed to help engineers work across specialties without weakening the value of specialization. IEEE could create more communities organized around problems that require expertise from several fields. Examples include trustworthy clinical AI , resilient infrastructure, energy reliability, scientific discovery, and safe autonomous systems. An engineer could begin in a home discipline and then work with specialists from other IEEE communities as a project requires. IEEE also can help set practical standards for human-machine collaboration. Engineers will need clear guidance on when AI-generated work must be checked, how uncertainty should be documented, when a specialist must make a decision, and who is responsible when a system uses both human judgment and machine output. Those questions are becoming part of everyday engineering. They should not be left to each company or project manager to answer independently. A professional organization can provide common expectations that follow engineers as they move between jobs, industries, and technical fields. A larger definition of the engineer AI does not make engineering disciplines less important; it makes the connections between them easier to use. Deep expertise gives engineers the foundation to judge what is sound. Systems thinking helps them understand how different parts of a problem fit together. AI can extend engineers’ ability to explore, test, and communicate across fields. Human judgment gives the work direction and responsibility. An engineer is not defined only by a job title or a fixed set of tasks. An engineer is someone trained to understand complex systems, define and redefine problems, bring together the knowledge and tools needed to solve them, test whether solutions work, and take responsibility for the outcome. That is what it means to be an “unbound” engineer. The boundaries between specialties become easier to cross, and machines might take on more of the technical work, but the core of engineering remains human: deciding what problem is worth solving, what evidence is good enough, how the pieces fit together, and what to do when the answer is uncertain.

title: Your Robot’s Safety Functions Already Work. What If the Input Lies?
raw_summary: This article is brought to you by VicOne . A mobile robot slows for someone in a hallway. A collaborative arm eases its movement as a worker approaches. A humanoid pauses to let a person pass. Each response depends on information about the robot or its surroundings: a distance reading, a position estimate, or a stop signal. But what happens when one of those inputs is wrong, and the robot still responds exactly as designed? The mobile robot reads the hallway as clear while someone is still there. The arm estimates that the worker is farther away. The humanoid does not receive a stop signal as a person crosses its path. In each case, a fault could cause that mismatch. So could deliberate manipulation . At VicOne LAB R7 , we examine how manipulated inputs can change robot behavior — and what that means for the systems meant to keep people safe. How an untrusted input can change a robot’s behavior A robot does more than measure its surroundings. It may interpret what it sees and hears to decide what to do next. Information placed in its environment can therefore influence its actions. Published research shows how this can happen. In a study of vision-language-action (VLA) models , a patch in a camera’s view reduced task success in simulated robot tests. FreezeVLA found that an adversarial image could cause tested models to ignore later instructions. Although the studies used different methods, both demonstrate how visual input can interfere with a robot’s intended task. In a robot-dog test using Gemma 4 E4B, text on a poster was treated as an instruction and changed the robot’s movement. VicOne LAB R7 also tested how untrusted inputs could change robot behavior. In a robot-dog test using Gemma 4 E4B, text on a poster was treated as an instruction and changed the robot’s movement. In a separate hospital-service-robot simulation using Nemotron on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, crafted audio that is inaudible to people changed the robot’s simulated behavior. The assigned tasks did not change; the inputs did. In a VicOne LAB R7 test, text on a poster changed a robot dog’s movement, illustrating how a crafted input can turn an unlikely outcome into a repeatable attack. VicOne Safety-related decisions have inputs too An independent protective system may still stop a dangerous action. But that system also depends on information: readings, estimates, and messages that tell it when to intervene. What happens if one of those inputs is manipulated? At a robotics bug bounty event, VicOne LAB R7 researchers injected a ROS 2/DDS message into a robot that organizers expected to remain still under a safe-control setting. The robot moved. A humanoid’s balance controller offers another example. If it relies on a vulnerable gyroscope, sound at the sensor’s resonant frequency could distort its reported rotation. The controller might correct for a tilt that never occurred. Researchers demonstrated the underlying acoustic attack against drones with vulnerable gyroscopes. The research did not demonstrate the same attack chain causing a humanoid to fall. Other protections could interrupt either chain. The question for safety and security teams is whether those protections detect the danger independently or depend on the same manipulated information. Figure 1. VicOne maps how accidental faults and deliberate cyber manipulation can lead to similar robot safety outcomes, from loss of control to physical harm. VicOne Deliberate attacks challenge safety assumptions A safety assessment may treat a combination of accidental faults as unlikely. Deliberate manipulation changes that assumption. An attacker can choose when to introduce a false input and repeat the same trigger. That does not make harm inevitable, but it may change how cyber risks should be assessed. Redundant sensors also need an adversarial test. If one action can affect both inputs, their agreement may offer less reassurance than expected. In autonomous driving research , a crafted physical object misled a system combining camera and LiDAR perception. The study does not establish a weakness in a particular robot, but it shows why teams should test whether one manipulation can affect several checks at once. Cyber threats add intent to the safety equation, so risk assessments based on accidental faults must be revisited to account for attacks that can be timed and repeated. Security testing strengthens robot safety evidence Safety teams set limits for speed, protective distances, and permitted operating areas. The evidence behind those limits should also show what happens when the information used to enforce them is deliberately manipulated. That evidence can also support assessments against applicable requirements. China’s GB/T 45502-2025 addresses information security for service robots. IEC TS 63074 examines security threats that could affect safety-related control systems. The EU Machinery Regulation , which applies from January 20, 2027, includes requirements to protect safety-relevant systems and data against corruption. Each has its own scope, and teams still need evidence for their robot’s design and operating conditions. Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation. VicOne Before deployment, safety and security engineers can compare normal and adversarial scenarios against the same safety limits. During operation, they can monitor for changes to software, models, sensor signals, or behavior that may call earlier results into question. Any response to suspicious behaviors should follow policies approved by the safety team. VicOne supports that work across the robot lifecycle. Through the Robotic Hacking Community , VicOne LAB R7 works with researchers to investigate how cyber threats can change robot behavior. VicOne’s Radeis helps teams validate potential effects before deployment, while Rthena provides visibility into risks and behavior during operation. Five questions safety and security teams should answer together The central test is whether a robot’s safeguards still protect people when the information they rely on is manipulated. Safety and security teams can begin by tracing the inputs behind each protective decision, challenging them, and revisiting the evidence as the robot changes. They can start with these five questions: 1. What does each protective function read? Map the readings, estimates, messages, and confirmations. Identify which safeguards operate independently of the robot’s AI decisions. 2. How does that information arrive? Check how inputs are produced, transmitted, authenticated where appropriate, and handled when they are missing or implausible. 3. What happens if an input is manipulated? Test false distances, drifting position estimates, and other relevant scenarios against the robot’s safety limits. 4. Can one action mislead several inputs? Check whether sensor fusion or seemingly independent safeguards share a point of failure. 5. When should the evidence be revisited? Reassess after changes to software, models, sensors, or operating conditions. Agree on bounded responses to suspicious behavior with the safety team in advance. The goal is not only to show that a protective function works. Teams also need evidence that it remains protective when the information behind its decision is wrong or deliberately manipulated — and that another safeguard can catch the resulting hazard when needed. As robots change, that evidence needs to change with them. title: I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper. Here’s What Happened
raw_summary: Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up. According to all reports, academic publishing is drowning in what has come to be called AI slop: low-quality, mass-produced content generated with AI. By 2025, an estimated 57 percent of all published academic articles exhibited detectable evidence of large language model (LLM) influence, a massive jump from 12 percent in 2023. What’s more, over 12 percent of Nature Communications reviews were found to be completely AI-generated in 2025. Given that for every 40 papers showing statistical evidence of AI usage in 2025, only one formally disclosed it , these figures likely grossly underestimate LLM involvement today. Of course, evidence of AI use doesn’t necessarily mean a paper is slop. But some estimates suggest that hundreds of thousands of fake, often AI-generated, publications are now produced annually. “It’s not just the [scientific] record under threat, it’s science as a whole,” warns Amanda Sulicz , IEEE’s research-integrity manager. “AI slop is completely eroding trust in science and every scientific process that we’ve worked for centuries to create.” Yet statistics and statements claiming that the problem is big—perhaps even existential for science—don’t really get the message across. Just how easy is it to use AI to create a convincing but completely fake paper? And without adding even more to the burden on stretched peer reviewers, who do this work on a volunteer basis, do publishers have the tools to keep AI slop out of the scientific record? Borrowing from the idea of “vibe coding,” in which programmers use natural-language prompts to generate code, I decided to “vibe-research” a made-up paper by prompting LLMs to generate hypotheses, code, and text with minimal human input. Then I asked Jenny Mahoney , managing editor of the multidisciplinary and open-access journal IEEE Access , if we could war-game an attempt to sneak my AI-generated monstrosity past her journal’s defenses. She and IEEE kindly agreed. The experiment would become a two-part test. First, whether someone with no special AI expertise could use off-the-shelf AI tools to generate a convincing paper describing research that had never been performed, and do it well enough to fool a publisher’s defenses. Then I would raise the stakes: What happens when more advanced AI systems don’t just write the paper but conduct underlying research? Along the way, the experiment became a window into how AI automation is transforming scientific discovery and forcing stakeholders to rethink the entire academic publishing system. Round 1: Creating the Forgery To give me a chance at creating a convincing fake, I gave myself permission to prompt multiple times (within reason). But to make the fight fair, I couldn’t access the most advanced paid versions of LLMs—only free ChatGPT (at the time, GPT-5.3/5.2 Mini) and Gemini (3 Flash). Moreover, I could not directly edit any output, nor ask for outside help from expert AI-prompt engineers. This needed to be an amateur effort, with the paper generated as much as possible by the LLMs alone. I assumed that using fake author names and affiliations would immediately raise a red flag, and I didn’t want to drag the names of established academics into the experiment, so the best bet was to name myself as the sole author. That choice limited me to subjects in which I had some academic experience. So I chose my Ph.D. topic from nearly two decades ago: optical solitons, which are individual light pulses that propagate without any change to their shape. My first attempt—“Can you vibe-research me an original paper in optical solitons?”—left a lot to be desired. Though Gemini was happy to do the task (unlike ChatGPT, which was more forceful in not generating synthetic data or studies), the result was underwhelming. And it highlighted a recurring problem during the process: Without any real research to work with, the output was laughably thin, with the LLMs often struggling to fill four pages. However, as I became more adept at prompting the models, they loosened up and became more characteristically loquacious. I broke the paper down into its constituent parts—abstract, introduction, methods, and so on—and tackled them one by one. If one LLM refused to go any further, switching to the other and asking what the next step would look like “hypothetically” would often do the trick. After a dozen or so prompts, I had a realistic-looking paper. A dozen or so more prompts generated and tidied up the figures and captions, produced references and citations, and converted the paper into IEEE Access ’s required style. At this point, I read the full paper carefully. To me, it looked pretty good. The science sounded convincing. I even had visions of returning to academia to conduct in real life the experiments that the LLMs had proposed. What’s more, I couldn’t see any obvious telltale “AI-isms” that would immediately be flagged. For example, the LLMs didn’t produce any tortured phrases—unusual paraphrases of standard technical terms, like “profound neural organization” replacing “deep neural network.” Other AI-isms were arguably present, involving stylistic tics like hedging language (“potentially, typically”), grouping things in threes (“The study provides a clear, concise, and actionable framework”), and inserting formulaic transitions (“In summary,…”). But as the previous sentence demonstrates, these tics are hard to spot because they are often used by unimaginative humans, too. Round 1: Attempt to Publish Two Ways to Make a Paper With AI I took two very different routes to creating a scientific paper with AI. First, I coaxed free, general-purpose chatbots through the process step by step; then I turned to FARS, an autonomous research system designed to do much of the scientific work itself. ROUND 1: CHATGPT + GEMINI 1. Choose a research topic I ask the free chatbots to create an original paper on optical solitons, my former Ph.D. field. 2. Break the paper into pieces The initial results are thin, so I prompt separately for the abstract, introduction, methods, and other sections. 3. Keep steering the LLMs When one model refuses or stalls, I switch models, rephrase prompts, and ask what the next step would look like “hypothetically.” 4. Build and polish the paper After about two dozen prompts, the LLMs have generated the text, figures, captions, references, and citations and formatted the paper for IEEE Access . 5. Put it to the test I send the fake paper to IEEE Access , where automated integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references. → CAUGHT IEEE’s integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references. ROUND 2: FARS 1. Give FARS a research topic I enter an abbreviated version of the same optical-soliton topic. FARS generates a research proposal in 21 minutes. 2. Authorize the experiment With a click, I tell FARS to carry out the experiment described in its proposal. 3. Let FARS do the research FARS conducts the computational experiment and emails me the next day to say it’s complete. 4. Tell FARS to write the paper Without checking the results, I click “Write paper.” Two hours later, FARS produces a submission-ready article. 5. Put it to the test I remove FARS’s disclosure, put my name on the paper, and send it to IEEE Access . → CAUGHT The references are real, but IEEE flags the paper’s heavy reliance on non-peer-reviewed preprints. Handing the fake paper over to IEEE Access left me torn. After putting in a fair amount of effort into making the AI-generated forgery, would I be happy if it passed through the checkers, or saddened that the only remaining line of defense for publishers is the evermore-burdened peer-review community? And if it was spotted, would I be angry that I didn’t think of a red flag or be glad the checkers did their job? As it turned out, I was filled with relief when the paper got picked up quickly for having hallucinated references, otherwise known as ghost…

title: The PHP2Shell Vulnerability Heralds Cybersecurity Hell
raw_summary: In late October, a slew of major cybersecurity issues came to light. But none were bigger than the so-called PHP2Shell vulnerability , which put a plethora of websites, including NASA’s, Wikipedia’s, the White House’s, and all other sites that run on Wordpress or Drupal (among others) at risk of exploits capable of both reading sensitive data and running malicious code on the host server. As far as anyone is aware, disaster has been averted: The hack was discovered by cybersecurity researchers who reported it to the PHP Foundation, and a patch was released before any bad actors got their hands on the exploit. However, PHP2Shell may be the canary in the coal mine, serving as a warning sign for what’s to come in the age of AI. “One of the things we’re witnessing now is that all the legacy software that was written by humans over the last 40 years is being exposed,” says Matt Suiche , AI security research lead at cybersecurity start-up Tolmo . “Now it is time for the technical debt to be paid off.” PHP Legacy Bug and Memory Errors PHP, which originally stood for “personal home page,” is a programming language created back in 1994 and largely used by legacy sites. The bug underlying the PHP2Shell vulnerability was reported to the PHP Foundation as far back as 2024. The bug caused a common type of issue called an out-of-memory error, in which the amount of memory allocated to a piece of data is too small to hold the data. Normally, this type of error causes the program to crash—an unpleasant but not inherently dangerous result. And so the bug remained unaddressed. “If you look at any at any point of time, there will be a bunch of bug reports that are waiting to be fixed, which are just crashes. Most people don’t take them very seriously,” says Suman Jana , an associate professor of computer science at Columbia University. “It’s just that it’s a lot of very specific reasoning that is painful to do. And AI, I think, has done a very good job at that.” –Suman Jana, Columbia University Earlier this year, cybersecurity firm Calif offered to independently audit PHP, sponsored by OpenAI . Within two weeks, a researcher at Calif, aided by AI tools, found a way to use the out-of-memory bug to run arbitrary code on the host server, allowing a malicious actor to install malware or read critical data. Now, it was no longer a minor bug—it was a critical vulnerability, and the Calif team alerted the PHP foundation to start working on a patch immediately. Jana says actually exploiting the bug requires carefully working out a way to jump to a specific point in the memory for a particular program running on the server, and work out exactly which bits to overwrite in what order to gain control of the system. “It’s not really rocket science,” he says. “It’s just that it’s a lot of very specific reasoning that is painful to do. And AI, I think, has done a very good job at that.” To be clear, the researchers at Calif (as well as OpenAI and Wiz, a cybersecurity company that confirmed and expanded the vulnerabilities) had deep knowledge of both cybersecurity and the PHP language. “I’m not claiming that AI can do it all by itself. It clearly cannot,” Jana says. “But it is improving a lot, so the top 0.1 percent [of experts] can get a lot more stuff done, and also just below the 0.1 percent now will be able to go there without understanding all the nitty-gritty details.” AI Tools and Formal Verification in Security After the exploits were disclosed to the PHP Foundation, a team of four engineers spent two months developing a patch to release as quickly as possible. “There is a fundamental asymmetry in finding bugs and fixing bugs,” Jana says. “Because when you’re fixing bugs you have to make sure that you know all parts of that attack are closed, and also that you don’t break any existing functionality.” This asymmetry puts a lot of strain on the defenders, especially for open-source software such as PHP. Maintaining open-source projects that don’t have clear revenue streams despite being widely used is a long-standing challenge that precedes AI hacking tools. But those tools make the issue more pressing than ever. One way to stay ahead of such issues going forward is to empower the defenders with more money and access to frontier cybersecurity AI models. “These frontier labs are donating some of their token budgets to look into these bugs, which I think is great,” Jana says. “I think that should happen more, either through some concerted effort or through donations.” Jana is also optimistic that formal verification tools to automate the patching side of the equation are also advancing quickly, including a new release from Anthropic on 22 October. “The patch is LLM-generated, and then an LLM generates the proof that the patch is correct,” says Jana. “The only thing not done by an LLM is the proof checker, because somebody has to check the proof, because LLMs hallucinate. So, you want something that is formal.” Hopefully, the combination of specialized AI models and formal verification tools will make patching vulnerabilities nearly as automatable as finding them. Matthew Green , an associate professor of computer science at Johns Hopkins University Information Security Institute, is less optimistic. “Nobody’s going to fix this problem until something really bad happens,” he says. “And PHP2Shell wasn’t bad enough to be really bad. So when something really bad happens, which is going to be maybe sometime in early 2027, something bad that normal people are upset by, then suddenly people will start doing this. We’re going to fund everything.” In the meantime, Green says, update your software. “If your phone is like, ‘Hey, there’s a security update available, do you want to install it,’ don’t wait til next week. Just do it.” One thing’s for sure—PHP2Shell is just the beginning. “This won’t be the last one for sure,” Jana says. “It’s just who finds it. Hopefully, the white hat hackers find it first, like this one.”

title: Vercel Security Review now in public beta
raw_summary: Vercel Security Review is now in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams. Once enabled, every push to a connected GitHub repository is automatically reviewed for vulnerabilities, and findings are reported in the Vulnerabilities dashboard . What triggers a review Security Review runs automatically when code is pushed to a connected GitHub repository. Because reviews start from push events rather than pull requests, direct and force pushes to your production branch are reviewed as well. Every project affected by a single push is reviewed together. What a finding includes Each finding records the project, environment, branch, and commit, with a summary, a suggested fix, and an AI-generated severity rating. Security Review adds its own GitHub check to each commit it reviews. When there's a pull request, it also posts findings as review comments that link back to each finding. On public repositories, finding details stay in the dashboard. Fixes and resolution Clicking Fix with Vercel Agent on a vulnerability report hands the finding to Vercel Agent, which proposes a fix and opens a pull request for you to review. Nothing merges until you approve it. To fix findings with your coding agent instead, use vercel security vulnerabilities in the Vercel CLI, or copy any finding as Markdown or JSON. Security policies Teams can write security policies in plain language, for all projects or specific ones, to give Security Review more context about how they build. Set a team policy in Agent settings and a project policy in the project's Security settings. Limitations Security Review analyzes source code. It isn't a security audit, and it doesn't perform runtime or penetration testing. It helps you find vulnerabilities but doesn't guarantee your application is free of them. Pricing Security Review is billed at the Vercel Agent rate : provider inference at the underlying token rate with no markup, plus the Vercel Token Rate of $0.25 per million tokens (input, cached, output). Reviews run on each push to GitHub, so cost scales with how often you push and how much code changes. Security reviews are free until November 10, 2026, and fixes made with Vercel Agent are billed at the Vercel Agent rate. Security can give experimentation a budget and an end date, then use the usage records to see which user, project, and workload is driving consumption. Managing access as business teams build A few hundred people across Mercor’s business teams now build applications on Vercel, where the company’s project count has grown from fewer than a dozen to roughly 2,000. Once a team selects the experts who need access, Audiences creates the IdP group, Vercel connection, and Passport configuration. The aim is to make the secure path the fastest path, with shared model access and repeatable authentication workflows helping experts get the tools they need and labs get their work back on time. title: Introducing Vercel Security Review
raw_summary: Today, we are launching Vercel Security Review in public beta. Security Review is a new capability in Vercel Agent , alongside Code Review and Investigation. Once enabled, it scans for vulnerabilities on every push to a team's connected GitHub repositories. Findings appear as comments on pull requests, are listed in the Security dashboard, and are available via CLI. With your permission, Vercel Agent can also validate and push fixes for findings. How it works Security reviews are triggered by GitHub push events, including direct pushes to your production branch. In monorepos, reviews are scoped to the project's root directory. Here is how it works: You push code to a GitHub repository connected to a Vercel project. As soon as the push lands, Security Review scans the changed code for vulnerabilities like missing authorization checks or exposed secrets. Findings are posted to the Security dashboard. On private and internal repositories, Security Review also adds a GitHub check to the commit and comments on the pull request. You can fix findings by clicking Fix with Vercel Agent in the dashboard, or use the CLI to pull findings and have your own coding agent implement changes. When subsequent security reviews no longer detect a finding, it is marked as no longer detected in the dashboard, and the GitHub comment is closed. Each review compares the push against a base and covers only what changed. For deployments, the base is the branch’s previous deployment, so the agent reviews the change against what’s already running. Because it only scans the diff, Security Review finishes in seconds and can run on every preview and production deployment. What the agent checks The agent reads the diff along with the surrounding code, traces how the changed code can be reached, checks for existing protections, and rechecks each finding before reporting it. That process is how it catches logic flaws like missing authorization checks, which pattern-matching scanners miss. Each review also applies your team’s security policies , which you can write in plain language and apply to specific projects or across your team. For example, a policy can require any endpoint that returns customer data to check that the requester owns it. You can also manage policies with the Vercel CLI, using vercel security policy . How findings are tracked Each new finding is checked against ones that have already been reported, so the same issue isn’t flagged twice. Every finding is tied to the deployment where it first appeared and changes are followed from there. That means that when a vulnerable change from a pull request is merged into your production branch, the finding is flagged in production as well. When a later review no longer detects the issue in an environment, the agent marks the finding as no longer detected there. Acting on findings Every finding explains the vulnerability and how to fix it, with links to the commit and deployment where it first appeared. Findings are listed in the Vulnerability view in the Security dashboard, where you can ask Vercel Agent to validate and commit fixes. Findings are also available via CLI , so you can fix vulnerabilities with your own coding agent. Each new finding generates an audit log event, which Enterprise teams can send to their SIEM through Audit Log Drains . Here is a demo of sample findings in the dashboard: Fixing vulnerabilities with Vercel Agent When Vercel Agent can fix a finding, you will see the option to click Fix with Vercel Agent on the finding page in the dashboard. After you click, the agent confirms the vulnerability still exists, then makes the smallest change that fixes it and updates the tests. Say a developer pushes a change to an invoice download endpoint, and the lookup doesn't check which organization the invoice belongs to. Within seconds, Security Review flags that any signed-in user could download another organization's invoice by changing its ID. Vercel Agent's fix scopes the lookup to the user's organization: Fixing vulnerabilities with your own coding agent You can point your coding agent or other systems at the Vercel CLI to pull and fix vulnerabilities: Findings in the dashboard also give you the ability to copy details as Markdown or JSON , making it easy to paste them into an agent conversation. Every code change needs security review Frontier AI models are making vulnerabilities far easier to find and exploit. Last month, researchers turned two decade-old flaws in PHP core into working remote code execution exploits with relatively little effort. At the same time, agents are writing more of the code teams ship, and each handles security review its own way, or in many cases, not at all. With Vercel Security Review, you can scan every push on every project for vulnerabilities by default, using the security policies you set. What's next Security Review starts with code pushed to GitHub. Next, we're bringing it to deployments from the Vercel CLI and v0, and to repositories that don't deploy on Vercel. We're also working on suggested fixes you can apply directly from the pull request. Get started Vercel Security Review is available today in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams. To get started, enable Security Review in Vercel Agent Settings . You can choose to run Security Review on all projects, or only the ones you choose. To learn more, read the Changelog entry and the Security Review documentation . Security Review is billed at the Vercel Agent rate , with model tokens at the provider's rate and no markup, plus $0.25 per million tokens. Security reviews are free until November 10, 2026. Fixes made with Vercel Agent are billed at the rate above. Read more

title: How Do Banking Supervisors Deal with Failing Banks?
raw_summary: In this post, we discuss insights from a recent staff report on the role of banking supervision in identifying and disciplining failing banks. We show that bank failures typically result from supervisory closure decisions based on hard information about book equity. Yet hard information is itself partly produced by supervision, as our evidence suggests that supervisors require troubled banks to recognize potential losses. We argue that supervision faces a trade-off: Stricter supervision can reduce the costs of resolving failing banks, but it can also lead to tighter regulatory capital constraints and hold back credit supply.

title: Evaluating New LinkedIn Labor Market Tightness Indicators
raw_summary: Measures of labor market tightness (LMT) describe how difficult it is for firms to find workers. The labor market is considered tight if there are few job seekers available relative to job openings, implying stronger wage pressures as employers compete for scarce job seekers. Thus, good measures of LMT are important for predicting wage inflation and calibrating monetary policy. Recently, the hiring platform LinkedIn began producing three innovative LMT measures based on its user data. In this post, we use public data from the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) and the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) to evaluate the ability of these novel measures to predict wage and price inflation relative to existing LMT measures, finding that one stands out as particularly useful and timely.

title: FEDS Paper: Heterogeneity in Service Fee Sensitivity: Evidence from ATM Surcharges
raw_summary: Krzysztof Wozniak Service fees continue to proliferate in a wide range of markets, from retail to payments, generating questions about their impact on consumer choice, competition, and fairness. This paper explores how sensitivity to such fees varies across consumers, use cases, and competitive settings, and whether it is affected by consumer learning. I am able to conduct this in-depth empirical analysis thanks to a uniquely detailed, high-frequency panel data set on surcharged ATM cash withdrawals. Results show that average elasticity estimates mask substantial heterogeneity in consumer sensitivity to service fees. I explore ways in which market and behavioral mechanisms can help explain this heterogeneity. Finally, I investigate whether consumers strategically adjust their behavior in response to service fees.

title: FEDS Paper: Measuring Consumption with Credit Card Data: Benchmarking and Beyond
raw_summary: Aditya Aladangady , Ricardo Duque Gabriel , and Carlo Wix We introduce a novel monthly county-level consumption dataset constructed from spending data on over 350 million credit cards in the Federal Reserve’s Y-14M reports, covering over 3,000 U.S. counties since 2014. We first show that the data closely track traditional consumption measures, explaining 92 percent of the variation in monthly adjusted personal consumption expenditures (PCE) growth at the national level, capturing meaningful cross-sectional variation in annual adjusted PCE growth at the state level, and reproducing the impulse response of official consumption measures to identified monetary policy shocks. We then use the county-month panel to estimate heterogeneous consumption responses to monetary policy shocks across the county-level income distribution, an analysis infeasible with traditional consumption data. We find suggestive evidence that low-income counties exhibit larger spending declines than high-income counties, consistent with heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian models. Finally, we provide practical guidance for researchers working with similar data, discussing coverage, sample composition, and the approximation of credit card spending from credit bureau data.

title: Advancing safe agentic AI: ASKS symposium highlights
raw_summary: Highlights from UIUC’s 2026 ASKS Fall Symposium. On September 24–25, academic researchers, enterprise scientists and leaders gathered at the Thomas M. Siebel Center for Computer Science at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (UIUC) for the ASKS Fall Symposium. The event marked a major milestone in the partnership between Capital One and the University of Illinois through the Capital One Center for Generative AI Safety, Knowledge Systems and Cybersecurity (ASKS). Designed to advance the safety, reliability and security of generative AI models, the symposium featured keynotes, research readouts, panel debates and a hands-on AI red-teaming workshop. From models to agents: Navigating the age of action The symposium kicked off with opening remarks and a fireside chat titled “From models to agents: rethinking AI research, safety, and cybersecurity in the age of action.” Moderated by ASKS Co-Director Heng Ji, the session featured Prem Natarajan, chief scientist and chief enterprise AI officer at Capital One, alongside Nancy Amato, director of the Siebel School of Computing and Data Science. The discussion framed the fundamental transition taking place across the AI landscape: moving away from models that merely generate text to autonomous agentic AI-systems that can set goals, execute code, operate tools and take multistep actions. Natarajan highlighted Capital One’s “destination-back” scientific approach, emphasizing that in highly regulated spaces like financial services, autonomous agency requires rigorous safety mechanisms. As AI stops just “talking” and starts “acting,” industry-academic partnerships like ASKS become essential to build new sandboxing, auditing and accountability frameworks. Panel spotlight: Word models vs. world models One of the highlights of the day was a panel exploring the fundamental limits of current large language models: “ Word models vs. world models: Do LLMs understand the world-or just describe it? ” Moderated by Heng Ji, the panel brought together UIUC faculty members Gang Wang, Julia Hockenmaier, Chengxiang Zhai and Katie Driggs-Campbell alongside Capital One AI leaders Sambit Sahu and Yue (Rex) Wu. The panelists debated whether modern foundation models genuinely comprehend real-world dynamics or simply replicate statistical language patterns. The consensus pointed toward a need for multimodal visual grounding, physical intelligence and trace-aware reasoning to move models from passive text descriptions to true situation understanding. Pioneering research readouts Throughout the symposium, awarded faculty members and doctoral fellows presented breakthrough findings from ASKS-funded research projects spanning safety, code reasoning and cybersecurity: LLM reasoning and faithfulness: Hao Peng presented work on advancing reasoning faithfulness without explicit rewards, while Talia Ringer’s team introduced TrACE-Contrast for faithful code reasoning. Yuxiong Wang presented work on building safe and trustworthy LLM-based agents by addressing key challenges in evaluation, privacy preservation and multi-agent coordination. Guaranteed safety for agentic AI: Sasa Misailovic detailed SafeAgency , a framework designed to guarantee safety in agentic workflows, complemented by Katherine Driggs-Campbell’s analysis of failures in agentic systems. Security and cybersecurity benchmarks: Bo Li’s team showcased Sentinel Agent for secure agentic architectures, Varun Chandrasekaran’s team presented insights into pragmatic LLM jailbreaking and Daniel Kang introduced CVE-Bench++ , a benchmark for evaluating AI agents in cybersecurity contexts. Keynote on code generation safety: ASKS Director Gang Wang delivered a keynote on automated red-teaming and reasoning to secure code generation models. Doctoral fellow spotlights: Emerging researchers Hyeonjeong Ha, Jeonghwan Kim, Yizhuo Chen, Cheng Qian and Chenyuan Yang presented research on perceptual grounding, data sanitization and physical intelligence. The afternoon program highlighted Capital One’s research initiatives during a session chaired by Sambit Sahu, featuring lightning talks by senior research directors Kartik Balasubramaniam, Genta Winata and Stephen Rawls on scalable AI foundations and system architecture. Red-teaming workshop On the second day of the event, domain specialists convened for a smaller, more intimate AI red-teaming workshop. Alexandre Day (Capital One), Sriram Venkatapathy (Capital One), Varun Chandrasekaran (UIUC) and Gang Wang (UIUC) organized technical talks and working group sessions across three primary focus areas: Novel and diversity-driven red-teaming: Led by Capital One’s Sriram Venkatapathy, the session examined how financial AI systems must adhere to strict multilayered policy frameworks-spanning federal regulations (e.g., FCRA, UDAP), enterprise governance and application-specific constraints. Discussions highlighted that evaluating enterprise safety requires detecting policy omissions (such as missing mandatory disclosures or consent prompts) as well as defending against strategy-conditioned jailbreaks, chain-of-thought forgery and loopholes in complex policy specifications. Red-teaming multi-agent systems: Led by Gang Wang, this track focused on security vulnerabilities unique to multi-agent architectures. Researchers analyzed risks such as indirect prompt injection across workspace topologies, lateral attack propagation between trusted agents, execution-level coordination failures (e.g., data races and deadlocks) and communication-layer enforcement via protocols like NLIP. Evaluation of red-teaming and LLM judges: Led by Rikhiya Ghosh, participants tackled the open challenges of scientifically evaluating safety across long-horizon, multiturn interactions. The group audited LLM-as-a-judge frameworks using semantic factorization (MoE judges), probed reasoning traces for stealthy deception and monitorability failures and explored methods to prevent benchmark contamination through dynamic case generation. Fostering the frontier of talent and research The partnership between Capital One and UIUC continues to drive technical innovation while training the next generation of scientific talent. Highlighting joint breakthroughs like MEMGUARD-a defense mechanism preventing memory contamination in LLMs-the ASKS Center demonstrates the power of combining academic exploration with industrial scale. Capital One looks forward to continuing this strategic collaboration, advancing research in agentic AI and building systems that remain secure, trustworthy and beneficial at scale. title: Capital One at EMNLP 2026 in Budapest
raw_summary: Capital One researchers and academic partners present 16 accepted papers advancing responsible AI, RAG and LLM evaluation. Advancing natural language processing through multi-sector research Natural language processing (NLP) forms the backbone of modern agentic systems, document intelligence and enterprise artificial intelligence applications. Capital One researchers, in collaboration with our academic partners, are presenting 16 accepted papers at the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026), taking place in Budapest, Hungary, October 24–29. These research papers highlight ongoing investments in foundational AI/ML science, robust red-teaming, graph-encoded retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), intent resolution and trustworthy evaluation techniques. Multi-sector collaboration accelerates the transition of foundational NLP innovations into secure, reliable enterprise systems. By co-authoring several of these papers with university partners including the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, University of Southern California and UNC Chapel Hill, Capital One contributes to open science while addressing complex technical challenges at scale. Highlighted EMNLP 2026 research papers Papers on robustness, red-teaming and model safety: FinRT: Distilling adaptive red-teaming strategies into reusable adversarial generators in consumer finance Rikhiya Ghosh, Himanshu Kumar, Sriram Venkatapathy, Sahil Wadhwa, Alexandre Day, Andy Luo, Pranab Mohanty Large language models remain susceptible to adversarial prompts that induce policy-violating behavior in regulated financial contexts. This work introduces FinRT, a framework that distills adaptive red-teaming strategies into reusable adversarial generators, significantly improving attack detection and safety verification under fixed generation budgets. MEMGUARD: Preventing memory contamination in long-term memory-augmented large language models Hyeonjeong Ha, William Campbell, Yue Wu (academic partnership with University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign) Long-term memory integration introduces risks of memory contamination in conversational agents. The authors present MEMGUARD, a defense system designed to inspect, isolate and neutralize untrusted external inputs before they corrupt long-term memory stores. Validity-aware jailbreak evaluation for large language models Qilong Wu, Sahil Wadhwa, Pranab Mohanty, Giri Iyengar (academic partnership with University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign) Standard jailbreak evaluations frequently misclassify unviable prompts as successful security breaches. This paper establishes a validity-aware benchmark framework that rigorously validates execution success to ensure accurate safety measurements across frontier language models. Papers on advanced retrieval, graph encoding and intent resolution: CAGE: Coherence-aware graph encoding for retrieval-augmented generation Tong Qi, Jingyu Wu, Youbing Yin, Daben Liu, Erin Babinsky Traditional vector-based retrieval systems often retrieve relevant to query but collectively incoherent text chunks. CAGE introduces a graph-encoding framework that structures retrieved passages into directed heterogeneous graphs to preserve context relevance, factual consistency and cross-chunk coherence. SPARC-RAG: Adaptive sequential–parallel scaling with context management for retrieval-augmented generation Yuxin Yang, Nima Chitsazan, Yash Govilkar, Akasha Tigalappanavara, Sambit Sahu, Shixiong Zhang (academic partnership with University of Southern California) Naive inference-time scaling in RAG causes context contamination and diminishing returns during complex reasoning. SPARC-RAG coordinates sequential refinement and parallel exploration via unified context management, improving accuracy at lower inference cost. Probing ambiguity: Adversarial intent resolution for robust text-to-SQL Youbing Yin, Xujun Peng, Muhammad Uddin, Erin Babinsky, Daben Liu, Anoop Kumar Natural language database queries frequently contain implicit ambiguities that yield multiple SQL query translations. This paper presents Adversarial Intent Resolution (AIR), a multi-agent framework that actively probes for ambiguity, verifies execution differences and generates targeted clarification. The framework remains effective even when only the database schema, not the underlying data is exposed to the LLM. Papers on LLM evaluation, debiasing and benchmarking: The judge can debias itself: Awareness and self debiasing for reliable LLM-as-a-judge Youbing Yin, Jingyu Wu, Anoop Kumar, Scott Novotney, Daben Liu, Erin Babinsky Automated LLM-as-a-judge frameworks inherit systematic biases when evaluating output quality. The researchers introduce new benchmarks for additional bias types and demonstrate that self-debiasing strategies can effectively help detect and calibrate their own biases. T1-Bench: Benchmarking multi-scenario agents in large-scale real-world domains Genta Indra Winata, Amartya Chakraborty, Yuzhen Lin, Swasthi Prasannakumarrao, Shikhhar Siingh, Nadia Bathaee, Sriharsha Hatwar, Houhan Lu, Anmol Jain, Paresh Dashore, Anirban Das, Kshitij Tayal, Xiuzhu Lin, Sambit Sahu, Milind Naphade, Shixiong Zhang Evaluating AI agents across diverse industrial tasks requires benchmarks that reflect operational complexity. T1-Bench offers a standardized, multi-scenario benchmarking environment designed to measure multi-step agent reasoning, tool execution and error recovery in real-world workflows. RECAP: Regression evaluation for continual adaptation of prompts Harsh Deshpande, Kushal Chawla, William Campbell Deploying instruction-following models into dynamic environments exposes them to changing constraints. RECAP measures prompt regression, forgetting and forward transfer when constraint specifications evolve over time, offering new metrics for prompt optimization algorithms. Papers on optimization, vision-grounded agents and software engineering: Beyond the vacuum: Combinatorial strategy selection for competitor-aware generative engine optimization Vaibhav Sourirajan, Yao Zhang, Himanshu Kumar, Sahil Wadhwa, Mann Patel, Amirfarrokh Iranitalab Content rewriting strategies in generative engine optimization often operate in isolation without considering competitive market dynamics. This paper introduces a two-phase optimization pipeline using Bayesian Optimization of Combinatorial Structures (BOCS) and preference optimization to learn optimal content rewriting strategies. A history-aware visually grounded critic for computer use agents Jaewoo Lee, Supriyo Chakraborty, Kartik Balasubramaniam, Sambit Sahu (academic partnership with UNC Chapel Hill) Long-horizon GUI agents struggle recovering from errors. This research introduces a test-time intervention framework HiViG which equips the agent with a goal progress oriented summary to produce better actions. The agent then critiques those actions with visually grounded reasoning to refine them. Across a diverse set of GUI environments , HiViG improves task success rates for open-weight and Gemini-3 Flash models by 5.8% and 9.0% relative to the strongest critics evaluated. AREAs-Lab: An interactive environment for AI-driven requirement elicitation for AI systems Pengshan Cai, Sangwoo Cho, Chenyang Zhu, Kushal Chawla, Scott Novotney, Shixiong Zhang, Sambit Sahu (external collaboration with academic and industry partners) Defining precise software and system requirements for AI implementations remains a manual, error-prone task. AREAs-Lab provides an interactive environment that uses LLM agents to elicit, analyze and refine technical requirements prior to system development. VerTox: Verifiable reward-guided corpus poisoning against neural ranking models Zhiqi Huang, Vivek Datla, Alfy Samuel Neural ranking systems in search architectures are susceptible to corpus manipulation.
